SULPHUR IN THE STARS.

Mr Norman Lockyer has announced the discovery of the strongest spark lines of sul phur in the spectrum of the bright star Rigel. These linc.s had not previously been traced in the sp rum of itny celestial body.* Cer- tain sulphur lines which behave in an abnor- mal manner in spark and vacuum tube •spectra are not found in the spectrum of Rigel, but they do occur in stars of the type of Bel'atria and Epsilon Orionis, which re- present higher stages of temperature than do stars of the type of Rigel.

The new issue contains the work of no less than 64 contril utors, comprising the most distinguished names in literature snd art, and all the illustrations are printed in_colonrs... . . . . .

In recognition of the efforts of the booksellers and newsagents of the country, a contribution will be again made from the proflts of the forthcoming issue, to the funds of the Newsvendors' Benevolent and Provident Institution and the Booksellers' Provident Institution. Another great feature of this issue is that it carries with it a free £l,coo Insurance, for three months, Against accidents to passengers in Motor 'Buses, Electric i ' Trams, &c. and this year, n response to many enquiries a beautiful cloth case for binding " Printers Pie " will le oh:Coble of Al Nexsagents and at the Railway Bookstalls.

div.head: GROWING A FOOT A DAY.
div.p: GROWING A FOOT A DAY.

During the long drought of the spring of 1907, in Mauritius, a singular spectacle, .amid the stretches cf dying and desiccated plants, was presented by the white flowers of giant aloe stems, which sprang up en the mountains and over the waste lancls with, amazing speed. At the time of flowering, shafts as thick as a man's arm shot up from the heart of the plants, grew from 12in. to 18in. in twenty-four hours, and reached a height of 30ft. A cluster of aloes before the flowers appear rosembles a gigantic asparagus plant.

div.head: TREMENDOUS RAINFALL.
div.p: A TREMENDOUS RAINFALL.

The astonishing effects sometimes- produced by cloudbursts are well known, but not manyl: trustworthy records of the depth of the rain- fall during such occurrences exist. The fol- lowing instance, therefore. pcEscsses much interest. On August 6th, 1906, during a thun- derstorm in the Fiji Islands, the measured depth of the rainfall in a gauge elevated 25ft. above the ground was 3ft. lir.. The rain con- tinued thirteen hours, and owing to unmea- sured owerfloiv, the total amount remains un- known, but it is estimated to have been not less than 41in.

div.head: EARTH'S CORE.
div.p: THE EARTH'S CORE.

Professor Wiechert, at a meeting of the Seismological Association at The Hague, as- sorted that his studies of the varying velocity of earthquake tremors, passing through the interior of the globe, lead to the conclusion that the earth consigsts of a cen- tral core of iron or steel, about 5,580 miles in diameter, surrounded with a stony shell 230 miles in thickness. Between the outer solid rind and the inner layer of rock, covering the metallic core, he thinks there is a layer of liquid, or plastic, material lying a little less than twenty miles below the surface of the earth.

div.head: PROPOSAL TO TAP VESUVIUS.
div.p: PROPOSAL TO TAP VESUVIUS.

When the channel of a volcano gets filled up with solidified lava there is a danger that the next eruption may shatter the monntrin to pieces. Fearing for Vesuvius a. fate similar to that , vvluch befell Krakatoa some years ago, Signor Coartino proposes to supply a safety valve. He suggests tapping the moun- tain by boring a tunnel at the base, and run- ning the lava into the fi?fl. He also points out hot* the liquid lava might be utilised bY running it into moulds, and thus making blocks for quays- and slaEs for paving the streets of Naples.

div.head: SOURCES OF ARSENIC.
div.p: SOURCES OF ARSENIC.

The most important sources of the world's supply of arsenic. are the silver mitre of Saxony, the tin and pyrites mines of Eng- land, and the mispickel (arsenical pyrites) mines of Spain and the Province, of Ontario, Canada. The Canadian mispickel contains gold. Germany now produces the greatest quantity of metallic and white arsenic, Eng- land, which led the world's production in DU, having since fallen behind. It is esti- mated that the United States consumes about half of the entire production of metallic, white, red, and yellow arsenic. The yellow arsenic is known as orpiment. In the arts arsenic is used in pyrote,ehny, and in the manufacture of shot, as well as for medicine and the making of fly-pm-tars.

div.head: SOUNDLESS ROOM.
div.p: A SOUNDLESS ROOM.

The Physiological Institute of the Univer- sity of Utrecht possesses one of the most re- markable rooms in the world, a chamber about 70. square, which is said to be abso- lutely noiseless, as far aa the entrance of sounds from -outside is concerned. It _is on the top storey of a laboratory building, and is an inside room, but is so arranged that it can be ventilated and inundated with sun- shine. The walls, floor, and ceiling each con- sist of half a dozen layers of different sub- stances, with air spaces and interstices filled with sound-deadening materials. Some per- sons when in the room experience a peculiar sensation in the ears. While every effort hoe been made to exclude sounds that are not wanted, of course the object of constructing this singular room was to experiment with phenomena connected with sound. Some of the sounds employed are made in th room itself; others are introduced from outside by means of a copper tube, which is plugged with lead when not in use.

NITROGENOUS DIET IN TUBERCULOSIS. In order to ,determine the effect of diet in tuberculosis, says the Scientific American, Lannelongue and Achard conimeneed by sub- mitting sixty male. guinea pigs of approxi- mately equal weights to the same regimen. Then all the animals ,were inoculated, in the pleura, with equal doses of the same culture of the bacilli of tuberculosis. The guinea pigs were then divided into three groups, of twenty each, "and to each group was given a special food in addition to the common diet. Each animal of the first group received. daily 9 grammes of butter, each of the sc!cond group 20 grammes of sugar, and each of the third group 20 grammes of gluten, Each of these increments had a food value of about 145 calories. The last survivor of the butter group lived forty days, the last of the sugar group eighty-seven clays, and the last cf the gluten group 371 days. or more than a year. These results of experiment cprrob6rate the earlier researches •of Lannelongue and Acharcl, and prove that nitrogenous sub- stances should enter largely into the diet of • consumptives.

div.head: DRESS-FASHION-HOME.
div.p: DRESS-FASHION-HOME.
THE QUEEN OF SPAIN'S NEW OED.

I King Edward is going to grant his niece, the Queen of Spain, one of the dearest wishes of het heart and confer upon her the blue ribbon Of the Order of the Garter. This, 'remarks the Taacr, is a mark of especial favour, as for more than six centuries now the Garter has not been given to ' any lady except the Sovereign Queen or Queen Consort of England. Queen Alexandra is at persent the only woman privileged to wear it. Queen Victoria Eugenie has fallen heir to some . magnificent jewels, by the way. On State occa- sions she wears a very high diamond tiara, which is said to be one of the most valuable in Europe. The front of ,her corsage• is covered with stars and orders, and round her neck is a • close-fitting nedclace or, enormous diamonds and a rope of pearls which reaches nearly to the i edge of her skirt.

div.head: BLUE SHANTTNG DRESS.
div.p: BLUE SHANTTNG DRESS.

A charming gown for afternoon wear is made of Nattier-blue Shantung. trimmed with bands of Oriental . trimming, embroidered in e3veral shades of the same blue. The bodice is cut low, and draped with a fichu-like collar, which is tucked on the shoulders, and bordered with trimming, crossod in, the centre of tlie front and back. The guimpe is of tucked ivory net over

white silk, and finished with a small pointed yoke and collar of ivory lace, a narrow frill of Valenciennes lace outlinin the point of the yoke. The sleeves are draped round the arm and bordered with bands of embroidery, the under-sleeves being of net, finished with little lace cuffs. The skirt is closely tucked about the hips, the narrow centre panel being carried up the front of the belt, which, by the way, is of soft blue taffetas, fastening at each side with a blue enamelled button. EMPIRE AND PRINCESS GOWNS. '

z'vidently war is waged between the Empire and the Princess costumes, or rather it would be more correct to say that intense rivalry e:cists between them. Perhaps this is cne reason, says a writer in the Globe, that so many of the new gowns are, in fact, a combination of the two. For instance, a very pale grey gauze gown v.-as Princess in front, the skirt very slightly draped below the waiat, while the bad: was entirely Empire, fastening with silk buttons the whole way from yoke .to hem, the latter finishing a graceful little train, not too long for ordinary--- circumstances, but certainly too long to be taken into a crowd like that at the Royal Academy. The graceful little lady who wore it had a white tulle ruffle, and her hat was black straw with terra-cotta feathers. Such a gown as thil can only be satisfactorily fastened by other hands than those. of the wearer. It would be impoasible for any. woman to hook or button herself into such a frock, therefore none attempt this style who does not possess a maid car at least obluring sisters. CLOTH WALKING COBTtNE.

Our sketch shows a smart walking costume, carried out, in tan-coloured cloth, trimmed with strappings of its own material, a very narrow black silk braid being placed at the inside edge of the strapping. The skirt is arranged in panels, divided by sets of pleats, the panels being trimmed with two • straps above the hem. no

little jacket, which meets only across the chest, and is much cut away in hind, is outlined with strapping, which is carried up tluX open side seams, the back portion being then wrapped over towards the front, and fastened with tan .suede-covered button.. The sleeves are wide at tlo armhole, and set in without fulness. They hare a strap of cloth down the outside, and finish with neat little turned-back cuffs. . A SUFFRAGETTE FAMILY.

Mrs. Panl;.hurst. whose name appears so often in connection with the I.Vomen's Suffrage Move- ment. is the widow of a gentleman who perhaps exercised more influence upon the passing of th.) Married Women's Property Act than anyone else. Her two daughters are in the very fore- front of the movement, for if Miss Christabel Pankhurst is the most eloquent of the Su2ragettes, Miss Adela may fairly claim to be the most enthusiastic. "No GLoviss."

It is all the grande mode in Paris now to be glOcless at evening functions. Gowns are so classical in character, so little fussy about the bodice, that anything so tailored as a glove looks ridiculous, besides utterly breaking the line of the arm and shoulder most inartistically. Of course, gloveless hands mean beautiful or well. kept hands. As for the finger-nails, they have become works of art and as artificially decora- tive as a jewel._ - -

div.head: 'lO-DAY'S RECIPE.
div.p: 'lO-DAY'S RECIPE.

POI:MET A LA YLAMANDE.—Take a fowl trussed as if for boiling, says a writer in the Daily Graphic. Wipe it out carefully with a cloth pre- viously rinsed in boiling water. Have ready two parboiled white-heart cabbages. Cut half a pound of either flank or streaky bacon into neat squares—not too small.. Place these in a and fry till the fat runs freely; then- add the fowl, together with half a pound of pork sau- sages, each sausage twisted into two smaller ones. Fry for ten minutes, turning frequently, so that the fowl becomes equally browned all'over. Then add a large onion, peeled and. thinly sliced, a bunch of herbs, and the cabbages. Add enough stock to cover the whole, and stew very gently for from an hour and a-quarter to two hours and a-quarter,:according to whether the fowl is very old or the reverse. When done, dish up the fowl, bacon, and sausages on a very hot dish, roll the cabbage in a cloth t'ahtiv end then cut it quickly into rounds. Thicken the stock wrrn an ounce of flour kneaded with an ounce of butter. Season to taste with pepper, salt, and half a irineglassful of sherry, garnish with the cab- bage, and strain the sauce over the bird through a heated gravy strainer. Serve with new potatoes.

div.head: Examiner Saturday, May. 16, 1908,
div.p: The Examiner Saturday, May. 16, 1908,
(Copyright.)
TIIE SENORITA'S DIAMONDS
Br WILLIAM WESTALL,
Author of "A Red Bridal," "A Woman Temptea Him," "Sons ci Belial," "With Vas lied Eagle," "Trust Honey," &c.
. i

I had promised Mrs. Canton, a gay young creole widow of Port-of-Spain, to take a packet for her to Carupano, a port on the Spanish Main, whither I was going on the business of ray Zan (Clordbn, Jones and Richards) for iviiich purpose I had chartered a droguer of some ten tons burd n. A drogner, I may mention, is a flush-decked,' slooped-rigged beat, without bulwarks

Mrs. Canton, on her Fat, had promised to bring the packet and eeo me off, and at .the appointed time cam with her brother, Mr. Lemaire, to the jetty, where the droguer was moored. The boat's name was Pallas, and she was sailed by two men, Paul Vert, the skipper, and Ileott r Macadam, a black Hercules with the characteristic features of his race. She had a tiny cabin aft where, though there was no standing -up, I could turn round, I cook my meals, and lie down, and a hole forward where the men might sleep, nun and turn about. There was also a diminutive dinghy, constructed to carry three. My friends came on board, and Mrs. Canton shewed great curiosity abaut my cabin, which she. inspected by peering down the hatchway. , "I should not like to sleep there," he remarked, with a pretty little sbcd ler. "If anybody were to put the lid on it would be as bad as being buried alive. You have not given Mr. Richards the packet, Robert.'" "Here it is, also a letter of introduction to Seiler Don Martino Veteran," said Mr. Lemaire. "The
packet is for his daughter 'end contains--"-

"Gems for the Seior La to. wear at a hall for which you will be just in thre,'" interposed Mrs. Canton. "They am, really superb, and if all Carupano does not go cmzy alratt them I shall Le much surprised. I ought to have let you see them. nov.ever, if you have any curiosity that way you are quite at liberty to gratify it ea route. Indeed, as you will have to smugee them through the Custom-house you had better undo the parcel and put the cases in your pockets separately.

- . I I did not quite like the cool way in which Mrs. Canto: assumed that I would risk the pains and penalties of smuggling - "for her beautiful eyes," but as I could never say "no" to a pretty woman I made no demur. We shook hands, she and her , brother recressed the gangway, the sails were l'unfurled, and as my barque bent-to the breeze they I waved their sunshades and wiThed me toss voyage. I The wind, though fair, was light, and by the time the sun went down, alinost without warning, we were threading our way among the barrier reefs of the Bocas, which rose like castellated heights, sheer from the water that lapped at their base end leaped up their sides .in tongues of light, for the sea had become phosphorescent, and then the moon rose—not the pale orb of temperate climes, but a glorious yellow globe, glowing in a purple sky—and wreathed the islets with garlands of gold, the splendour of the scene was so overwhelming as to seem rather of heaven than of earth, and so like fairyland that snore than once I asked myself whether I still lived—in the'llesh. : I stayed on deck the greater part of the night, only turning in about an hour before dawn. When I awoke we were moving slowly along the Venezuelan coast. But for the current, the set if which thereabouts is always westward, we should scarcely have moved at all, the breeze having almost died out. As the day wore on the heat increased, and the calm became so complete that we made no way what- ever. I beguiled the time by reading, smoking, and talking with Paul Vert; and bethinking me, after a . while, of Mrs. Canton's commission, I dived into my cabin, ,undid the packet, and opened the cases. The splendour and variety of 1113 gems astounded sue. As the little knowledge of such things— brooches set in diamonds, bracelets, rivieres, pearl necl I ices and the rest—l possessed had been gained by looking into jewellers shop windows, my esti- mate of their value was necessarily somewhat vague. I But I felt sure they were worth several thousand I pounds. Seilor Estevan must be a wealthy man to be able to make his daughter so magnificent a present. Then it occurred to me that the gems might merely be hired. Jewellers were always ready to lend -their wares for a special occasion at a special price. Be that as it might, I was very angry, both with royself and Mrs. Canton. I ought not to have , taken charge of the packet without knowing soine• thing of its contents and their value, and she ought not to have given me an onerous and, possibly, 3 dangerous commission without mentioning the risks . .

and responsibility it would involve. She might well want me to smuggle the things through the Custom-house. The duty would run into a big figure, probably more than the money in my posses-ion would enable me to discharge, and if I were detected I should be arrested and heavily Not a pleasant prospect, but as Hrs. Canton had said, I could put the cases itito my pockets, which the officers were not likely to search. Raising my head as I replacid them in my Glad- stone bag I saw Vert glancing e owl.. with a strange look on his weather-beaten face. But as he \vas at
the helm and, therefore, nearly over my head—and curioaity is a venial offence—l attached no im- portance to .the incident, though I had reason to _ .

Chink a good deal of it afterwarils. Again I spent the greater part of the night on deck, not going below until tbere came a light sea- breeze which, by coolirg the air, made sleep possible. I slept soundly, and as I knew when I awoko, slept long. But to my great surprise I was in pitch darkness, end bathed in rerspiration. The little cabin was like an oven. "Confound it, one of those fellow S has tattened the hatch down," I thought, and with that I got up and tried to unship it. Whcnin utterly failing shouted my loudest, and no heed being given, stamped with my feet, hammered with my hands and made al if the noise I could. _ _

All in vain. lsia;e-dry. -answered. The fate fore- shadowed by Mrs. Canton bad overtaken toe. I was buried alive. Vert had overheard Ihe talk about the diamonds and seen them when I opened the cases. Rot though it was I shivered with fear, and the booming' of the surf en the lonely rock- bound shore sounded in my ears like a knell of death. Hastily and with trembling fingers I struck a watch, lighted cry lamp, and looked round the cabin. The Gladstone bag was gone, also, no doubt, were Vert and the negro, perhaps after scuttling the felcop. It was clear that unless I meant to die like a rat in a hole, I limit be out of the cabin within the next few minutes. But how? Bursting the hatch open by sheer strength was impossible, and I had neither crowbar nor hatchet. Yet—and the-thought revived my drooping courage—l had something that might serve in their stead, a revolver, n rereiting rifle, a pockett-saw and a broad-bladed knif.

Rapidly loading the revolver I tired it six times through the hatcl), then reloaded it and fired again, making a square of twelve holes close together. Next, with illy-hunting knife and the pocket-zaw, I cut the pion out, thereby forming an opening through li:eh I cold put my arm and remove the bar that f tstened the hatch. My first glance when I gained the deck was rstern. The dinghy had di,appeaed, and away to the north I dnenered what looked like a small boat, in which, I felt sure, wtre. the rtnlians who had robbed and deserted me. Only the jib was sot, and the sloop was drawing dangerously near the breahers. Th.,ugh a complete duffer as touching sminanship I could steer, so taking the tiller I put the aroguer's head north- west. I had now time to think, ' and was wondering whether I should be able to it .vigate the Pallas to Campania and how scoa I might hope to get there, when I saw a thin rointnn.of.smoke coming out of

the fo'entsle. This was distinct and after 'hurriedly lashing the tiller to a stanchion I ran forward to see what was the matter. Fire was the matter. Befcre leaving the sloop Vert and his man had evidently lighted a fire in their cabin, but whether accidently or by design, in such a way that it would smoulder for awhile l.efore In:eking out, as it was just on the point of Sty drst impulse was- naturally to put oi ofit, and taking a bucket 1 set myself to the..,worA with snch frantic -nergy that in a few minutes flue place was full of kto :n, the best of ere extinguishers, on which I ret,,ned to the helm and put the bipat I eforo the wind which, albeit light, vtas blowing in the right direction, almost due west. This done. I wiped the perspiration from my eyes and looked seaward, when, to my amazement, I pert eivvd that the dintthy had nut abort and was atiing towards no. awl as we were approaching curb mher, would Soon be alongside. What this mtpaceuvre might portend was by no means clear.
but in order to be prepared tor eventualities, I loaded my rifle and - revolver and placed them within reach.
Meanwhile the boat ca;ne swiftly on, both the men pulling for all they were worth. "What do yon want " I shouted, so soon as they were within bail. ;

No answer being veuchsared, I repeated the question, whereupon Vert looked round, spoke a word to Macadam, and went on rowing, if possible, ! harder than ever. I le'. them come within a stone's throw of the sloop, then sung out again. "What do you want? If you don't stop and ariswcr, I shall shoot," at the same time raising the rifle to my shoulder. "I have something very particular to say, and I want to. come on board, said Vert, resting on his oars.

"And so yt:u alkali, bnt on conditions," I answered. "You are a sordid, murderous scoundrel. Not content. with robbing me, you tried to destroy all tract of your crime by burning the sloop and me with it, end the fire having missed you want to come on board and kill me."

"So help me--" "There ix no need to swrar. I would not believe you on your oath, and I won't hear a word. It would serve you right to shoot you right off, and I have a good mind--" Vert made a sign to the ne
ani be

mikllff a Sign backwater with one oar nod row with the other. j "Stay where you are and hear what I have to say—or take the consequences," I added, still , pointing my rifle. \ After a moment's hesitation Vert did as he was told. "Now, these are my orders," I,went on, _ obey

, . . . them promptly and I shall spare your lives, disobey and I shelf shoot you with as little compunction as I would shout a mad dog. You will come alongside, and let Macadam bind- you hand and foot, and lift you on board. Then he will make fast the dinghy and follow you, and tinder you: directions hoist the mainsail and put the sloop on whatever course I desire. But I shall keep the helm and have my revolver handy, and if Macadam ' tither disobeys mo or tries to release you, I will shoot you both." • "Will you kindly listen one moment? " By way of shutting the rascal's month and bringing him to reason, I fired a shot that struck one of his oars and narrowly missed his hand. This settled the matter. "I will do as you wish," he - said, "but if you will believe me, Mr. Richards--" _ I

"I don't believe you, and you will be good enough to speak cnly when I ask you a question. Come alongside." Which vas done; I threw a cord into the boat and saw that Vert was effectually bound. Macadam then brought him and the Gladstone bag on boi!rd and moored the dinghy astern. "How soon can we get to Caminito ? " I asked.

"Before sunset, if tiiis wind "And how soon to Port-of-Spin ?" "Goodness knows. The wind would be dead against us, we should have to make a long fetch towards Tobago, then there would ke getting through the Bocas."

"Two days?" "At least; more likely three or four." "In th.,t case I shall•go to Carupano, so shape our course accordingly. Tell Macadam what to do so as to get there as quickly as possible, and I shall follow your directions about steering, only if you want to keep a whole skin, hold your tongue, and don't try to play any tricks." I had been in some doubt as to whether it were better to give the villains up to justice at Port-of- Spain or Carupano. Other things being-- equal, I should have preferred Pcrt-of-Spain, but there were potent reasons against returning thither, even if I could afford the time I was by no means sure that the colonial authorities could or would 'take cognisance of a crime committed in Venezuelan waters; and it would be impossible for me to re- main on deck for three or four days and nights with the tithr in one hand and a pistol in the other. So there was nothing for it but completing my voyage to Carnpano. How I should act when I got there was not quite so obvious. I had an idea that Venezuelan justice was in a very rudimentary state ; I had hand that the •office of judge was cfren exercised by bakers, butchers, and candlestick- makers, and I. feared that. if I had Vert and Macadam arrested I might be detained foi• weeks and put to great expenqi and trouble. Moreover, I had no witnesses, and as the prisoners would deny whatever I affirmed, a conviction was extremely improbable. They might even turn the tables by bringing a charge against me, so recalling that useful ,and sagacious test : "Agree with thine adversary quickly," I decided to come to an accommodat ion with Me. Vert, to which end—the sails being Pet and the sloop settled on her course— opened a conversation with the gentleman. "I thought you were an honest fellow, Vert," I said. "You looked it, and Mr. Lemaire gave you an excellent character." "I was an honest man, sir, as honest a man as there is in the West Indies, un!il. I saw these diamonds, and the devil whispered in my ear as there was a fortune for the taking, and that I had only to stretch out my hand to be worth twenty thousand dollars."

"So you sold your soul to the devil and devoted me to destruction for twenty thousand dollars!" "Yes, sir. I acted like a villain, only lam not quite so bad as you think. I had no sooner quitteC: the sloop than -I began to rue what I had done, and I came back—not as you suppose, to murder you, but to save you and ask your forgiveness." "Why did not you say so, then?" „

. - "You would not give me a chance. You would not hear nic. Ask lice or if I'm not. telling thetruth. " "It is true, llr. Richards, as trite as I live," put in the negro. "Cap'n Vert, he say it was the ole devil had tempted him, that if he did not go back and let you out of the cabin and ask your for,giveneqs, something bad would happen to him, and he would.never-know a moment's peace as lowg as he lived." . - -

"and something bad ought to happen to you, Vert. You ought to be hanged, and I'm afraid you are lying. However, you may take the benefit of the doubt. As soon as we sight Carupano. you shall be loosed and I shall bring no charge against you." Vert, with tears in his eyes, protested infinite gratitude, saying I was a Christian gentleman, and. that he would never forget my kindness. On which bade him F hut up, and thinking presently that he had been sufficiently frightened, and my steering being none of the best, I released hifn and let him take the helm.

Yet I was by no means convinced of the sincerity of his repentance, thinking it very likely that if I had not got out of the cabin I should have been left to perish. The pistol shots, which he must have heard, had apprised him of my escape, na which he returned to complete his work, and hut for the measures I took, would probably have done so. On the other hand, it might Le that Vert had tine:imbed to a suddsn temptation, and I felt that I was to blame for letting him see the gents of which I had been so ill advised as to take charge. They had turned his head, and though he had been basely treacherous, he had not acted like an old offender. A thorough-wed villain had knocked me on the head as I lay asleep in the cabin. ,It was 5150 possible, as he protested, that the fire had been arcideatal. Anyhow, he had acted more like an amateur in crime then an adept, and I saw no cause to rue my decision not to prosecute him. Nevertheless. I continued to watch him closely, and felt greatly relieved v.hen at four p. in. we let go near the jetty at CartipAno. I went ashore in the dinghy, having previously bestowed the jewellery in try pockets, and as I squared the adminstrador with a doneur and his subordinates with a box of prime cigars they made only a ceremonial examination of my baggage. Vert said he should stay at Carupanu to or three days, on the off-chance of getting return freight ; and after settling with him I made my way to the posada, engaged a room and changed my clothes. Then, being anxious to get rid of my dincerous charge so -soon as might be, I procee ed to the house of Senor Estevan, presented my lettier of introduction, and gave him Ilia cases, wind' I had repaced in the original package. JJe was a veny courteous gentleman, profuse in his thanks, and pressed ire to make his house my home during my stay at Carupano, an invitation which I gladly accepted, for the accommodation at the inn lefta great deal to be desired. This point being settled 1 was introciuced to Senora and Set-loran Estevan, the latter a charming LiA of seventeen summers, nith great black eyes, an oval face, is clear olive complexion and is superb figure. She and her mother asked after Mrs. Canton and thanked me effusively for the trouble I had taken in bringing the jewels. I answered, not very veraciously, that it had been much more of a pleasure than a trouble, and that I felt greatly obliged to Mn. Canton for giving me an oppor- tunity of making their acquaintarce. The Mill was a fancy Aresa affair, and would take place in three days. Miranda ((lie young lady's Christian name) was to figure as the Queen of Sheba, her father as King Solomon. With some difficulty (the time being short) I obtained he to fume of a caballero of the ancien reliime.

I need hardy say that Senorita Estevan was the belle of the ball. That. Was iti raison d'être. Moreover, her get-up was wonderfully picturesque, and her diamonds created quite a sensation. People could not take their eyes off her and them. But while some of the guests were loud in their admiration of the young lady's beauty others were equally free in their condemnation of her father's extravagance, saying that he was a mighty fool to spend half his fortune on the adornment of his daughter. But Don Martino seemed more than satisfied with his investment. His face was all smiles, and he received the felicitations of his friends on the Senorita's success and her brilliant appearance with Unaffected delight. Dancing went on till nearly dawn and until the last of the guest were gone none of the family went to bed, with the necessary result of a late breakfasr, that is to say, late for Venezuela, whore people generally rise mith the sun and breakfast as soon as they rise, I was in the verandah, which enclosed the patio or inner court, soon after eight, and there found my host. "The ladies era breakfasting in their own rooms," said be. "Ours will 138 served here." As it pre- sently was, a light repast of arepa (maize cakes), coffee, and biscuits._ _ _

We' were soon through with it, and had just lighted our cigars when the administrador of the customs and two shoeless and coaticss soldiers, with fixed bayonets, marched into the patio. "We are come on an unpleasant errand, Saner Estovan," said the administrador. "Information has been given to the Senor Judge that this gentle- man (poining to me) brought a large quantity of jewellery eshore last Tuesday without declaring the same. 'As Senor Judge has likewise been informed that the jewejlery is now in your possession. We are here to demand its surrender and conduct you to the court-house, to be dealt with as the Senor Judge may decide and the law prescribes." This, for which I had, doubtless, to thank that rascal Vert, was very unpleasant. I foresaw a long detention and a lot of trouble, and felt seriously annoyed that I had been placed in se) false a posi- tion, and the cool way in which Don Martino took it all added to my vexation. He seemed more amused than surprised, and asked the administradcr, with a smile, whether we were to consider ourselves under arrest. • "I am afraid so," was the answer. _

"Enough! We will go with you, and if you will come to my room you shall have what you want." iAs soca as the custom's man was n posSession of the gems we wrre walked otT between the two soldiers, whose uniforms consisted of trousers and shirt, the latter worn outside the former.
The court-house was situr.:y a large room with bare walls, five or six chairs, and a table, at which sat the Senor Judge and another personage, whom I took to be his clerk. .

- Both of them were in their shirt sleeves and each of them sported a large cigar. I had thrown mine away, but Don Martino was still smoking. After an exchange of courteous greetings, for everybody was exceedingly polite, the adruinistrador stated the case, on which the judge asked me if I had ought to say. As there was no disputing the facts all I• could do tvas to plead guilty and throw myself on the mercy of the court, though I did not put it quite in that way, merely saying that, being a stranger, I was naturally ignorant of the laws of Venezuela, which I great ly regretted having unwittingly broken. The judge conferred with the gentleman I had supposed to he his clerk, but who, as I afterwards heard, was merely a neighbour that was able to read and write, accomplishments which the judge (elected by universal suffrage) unfortunately lackec!. "That is no excuse," he said, severely. "You ought not to be ignorant of the laws of Venezuela. The gems belong to,Don Martino?" "They do. Senor Richards was good enough to bring them for me," put in Don Martino. "And you knew they had not paid duty?" "Si, Senor Judge." The value of the jewels is very great, several thousand dollars?"

"Possibly. Dot as you would not accept my estimate of their value you had better consult an expert." On this another conference, and a reference by the amateur clerk to the code, after which the judge,rfronounced judgment. Don Martino and 1 were to be fined five hundred dollars each, and unless this amount, as also the ,duty, roughly estimated by the administrador at another thousand dollars, were paid in fourteen days the gems would be confiscated to the State. "So that is your decision," said Serior Estevan, quietly.: "If I don't pay two thousand dollars within the time mentioned—l cannot, of course, lct my friend pay any part of ,it—you will keep all those pearls and brilliants P" "It is my decision, Hon Martino, and. strictly according to the law," replied the judge, glaring greedily at the cases; which lay ore's on the table. "You may keep their, then. They are all paste, and not worth fifty dollars." -To know you have been used as a spoon handle does not, in ordinary circumstances, snake for mirth, but the judge and the odministrador, who had no doubt reckoned on squeezing Don Martino for their mutual benefit, seemed so dumbfounded and undone that I thirst out laughing; as did also the ten or a dozen individuals who composed the audience,—except Paul Vert, who looked as if he bail seen a ghost. "All pastel Not worth fifty dollars! How are we to know that? " demanded the judge, when he had recovered from the shock. • -

"Mira!" (look) answered Senor Estevan, taking a rope of pearls from one-of the cases and crushing them in his en;ers. Common glass! Here is a diamond bracelet worth, if the brilliants were real, five thousand dollars. It would look well on your daughter's arm, etSiior Judge. Do me (ho favour of accepting it, on her behalf ; for, after all, these things are still mine. Is there any duty on :flash jewellery, Sefior Administrador ?" "Twenty per cent. ad valorem," replied the officer, surlily. "On the wholesale _price, of course ; say, thirty dollars. Well, if you like, I will redeem the lot on that basis and pay in addition a small lino, though I think my friend may wdl be excused for supposing that bogus gents are not dutiable," After still another consultation, tl:e judge announced that if Don Martino would pay n fine of twenty dollars he might take his property away, with him.

"Too touch by half. However, as things have go)te so far let it be as you say," answered Don Martino. "Here is the money. You aeocept the bracelet of course, Scrier Judge, and the Sella. Administrador will p:rhaps chlige me by aceepting this:diamond ring for his wife, Adios Senores." And with that my host resumed possession of his property, and we went away, arM-in-arm. A thought struck me. "Are all those things false, Becior Estevan?" I asked, in an under!one. "Not all, by any means, and if the judge had persisted in his first decision, I am afraid I should not have got dr for much less than ten thousand dollars."

div.p: PA DGATE.

INDUCTION or TIIE NEW VICAR. —The Rev. Gerald William Dickinson was instituted by the Right Rev. the Lord Bishop of Liverpool and inducted by the Ven. Archdeacon of Warrington to the benefice Christ Church Padgate on Tuesday evening. Notwithstanding the miserab!o weather, a large congregation assembled. There was a good attendance of local and district clergy including the late Vicar (Rev. W. Pollock Bill). The usual form of service was adopted and several hymns specially selected for the occasion were sung, Mr. P. Blackwell presiding at the organ. The Bishop, in this early part of the service, preached from St. John xxi.l7 " lie saith unto him the third time, Simon, son of Jonas lovest thou me ? Peter was grieved because he said unto hire the third time Lovest thou me. And he said unto him, Lord, thou knowest all things ; thou know eat that I love thee. Jesus earth Into him' Feed my sheep." Baying alluded to the importance of the new Vicar feeding the lambs of Christ's flock, the Bishop said he hoped the Vicar would also feed the sheep. It was the duty of the Church of England clergy to visit their people in their homes and, if possible, from house to house. Ile believed in the old saying that "A house- going parson makes a church-going people." In con- clusion the Bishop asked the parishioners to rally round their new Vicar, give him a fair trial and bear up his hands, so that they might Lill the church to overflowing. *WESLEYAN SUNDAY SCHOOL.—On Sunday the anniversary sermons were preached in the IVesleyau Church by the Rev. Thomas Ross, of Doncaster,a former minister in the Warrington circuit. Mr. Russ was a great favourite with the young people during his ministry in that neigLhouthood fifteen years ago and large congregations assembled to hear him on Sunday. At the children's flower service held in the afternoon the Rev. Thomas Miller gave a useful address on bird- nesting and its cruelty. Mr. George Weaver, of Warrington, presided. Some of the Sunday School scholars recited chapters of tl.e Bible as lessons for tat) service. Misses Duckworth and Rrough each rendered snored solos very sweetly. Thechildrebacqnittei them- selves splendidly in the special hymns they sang and I reflect great credit on the conductor Mr. Cutland. Mr. I Thigh Mellor was the organist at all the services. The offertories on behalf of the Sunday school, amounted to £22, but it expected that this will be augmented.

div.head: • NEW BRIGHTON TOWER.
div.p: • NEW BRIGHTON TOWER.

• NEW MANAGEMENT AND NEW ATTRACTIONS AT TIIIS I'OPULAR RESORT. More peeple visit New Brighton than go to Blackpool every season, and the popularity of this resort is secona to DO other place in England. The great Tower and its imany attractions in the building and gardens be been a potent drawing attractions to many thousands every summer' but of recent years the search after novelty has not been very successful and the same things have been offered season after season. For the present year I Ms. John Calvin-Brown. Yanaging Director of the Whits City at Manchester, has taken over the liTannge- meat of the Toe er and has introdueed many new and striking novelties into its attractions. The prin- cipal of these new things will be the big Cummins-Breen] Wild West, ehich will occupy the ! Athletic Grounds and will give performances every afternoon rind ovening during the summer. In this show the life of the Rod Indian both in peace and war will be illustrated by song, dance, battle, etc., just as this same organization showed it under supervisicn of the United States Government at the great International Expositions at St. Louis, Buffalo and Omaha. In addition the programme will consist of bucking horses, riding by some of the most expert Cowboy riders in , America, Stage Coach attacks, quadrilles on horseback, roping and tying of cattle, sharpshooting and fine markruanship by expert men and women riflemen. The Wild West will be a gr. at place of popular amusement and the biggest single attraction ever put in a park. In the Tower Theatre Miliican's Old Plantation Show of negro singers, dancers, actors and coon shouters %lilt be seen every afternoon and evening. In the grounds a number of new devices and shoes have teen added to the popular Water Chutes, Hales Tours, Air Ships, Himalaya, Railway, etc , etc. The test of these new things are the Scenic Rail ri ay with nearly rt mile long ride encircling the lake the Figure 8 gravity Road on the front near the Promenade and next to the other big side the Areo Flyte, and these are backed up by the Old Light House, the 0.1.0. Cyclss, the Helier Skelter, the Swinging Switch Cars, etc., etc. r The Crimmins-Brown famous Wild West Cowboy Band will give afternoon and eveniog Free Concerts on the Plaza every day. The Ballroom will open as trust all day for dancers. The Billiard rooree, rifle galleries, Mali shows, illusions, etc., etc., will be going en all the time, and the refreshment rooms, cards end tea rooms have been arranged in style and prices to catch popular fancy. Many changes have been made in the arrangement of the giounds, and all looking toward the errhancoment of Its beauty and the comfort and pleasure of visitors. No other Park in the world is so favoured by nature, and no other contains so many and so varied attractions, hence it is safe to predict fur the Tower and its new management a highly successful season. Saturday, lAray 23rd, is the opening date.

div.head: OUR LOCAL CHURCHES.
div.p: OUR LOCAL CHURCHES.
Sankey Bridges Wesleyan Sunday Wool.

Anniversary Services in connection with this Sunday aohool were held on Sunday and were attended with success. The Rev. Harold C. Morton, of Derby,preached to a good congregation in the Wesleyan Church in the Morning, and gave an interesting sermon on the pessi- mistic parables of Jesus Cnrist. In the afternoon a musical service was held at Parr Hall, when special hymns were sung by the choir and children under the leadership of Mr. C. R. Muir. Mr. E. S.Mickers was the organist. Miss L. Fairhurst gave an expressive inter- pretation of" Nearer, my God, to Thee." The singing of the choir, children, and soloist was greatly enjoyed and Mr. C. E. Parker, who presided, and the Rev. B. J. Gawne, who was the speaker, gave unstintsd praise to -them and the conductor. In the evening, there was a large congregation in Parr Hall when the Rev. • The Sunday School Anniversary Services were cele- brated in Creekids' Dining Hall on Sunday. Keen- slderable amount of interest was centred in a scholars' Procession which preceded the morning service. A large number of scholars and adults assembled at the school and paraded the district,singiug hymns at various Points along the route. Favoured by grand weather this initial attempt proved a great success. The preacher for the day was the Rev. George Evers, of Baptist College, Manchester. At the morning service,, which WIS held in the chapel, he delivered a splendid sermon- ette to the children based on the word "Light." the afternoon a musical service was held in the Dining Hall. A large congregation attended. Captain George Crosfleld presided, and in the course of a few `remarks emphasised the point of playing the man. Special music was rendered by the children and choir, also the anthem "The house of the Lord. The speaker Was Mr. G. Davey Smith. He delivered an eloquent address on the great need there is at the present time ,of parents and Sunday school teachers paying great attention to the finer training of the children. The evils of the day could not be overcome unless those who were responsible for the teaching of the children taught them What they meant. Several evils. were shunned by 'teachers and, parents on the grounds of modesty, yivi the result that many of our young Inc in(' women were turned out on the world Iriorant of what they had to face. The hall . 'naks.erowded at the evening service. Mr. Evans took a.a" "la test " And Samson wist not the Lord had !Parted from him," and " Moses wist not that the skin ut_ his face shone." Carefully portraying the characteis r" these two Biblical heroes, the preacher drew maly suns pertaining to the lives of individuals of the Rresent age. The pleasures of the world were constantly 11110 downfall of many people, while striving at the same 'lmo to play their part in life. It was only by the con- secrated service that man would sucOeed. •Great praise Must be accorded to the children and choir for their Performance during the day. The singing was sweetly /"ndered and reflected great credit on the indefatigable Veils of the choirmaster (Nfr. F. Atkinson). Master A• Tanner presided at the organ, while an orchestra aOder the leadership of Mr. H. Vane added very largely to the musical part of the services. Stockton Heath Wesleyan Church. Sunday School Anniversary.

Special services in celebration of the Sunday school anniversary wore held at the Stockton Heath Wesleyan Church on Sunday-. The preacher w2S illo ROC'. S. T. Bosward, of P.III, whose discourses were listened to with much interest by large congregation,. At the morning service he took for his text the words : "My little children, let us not love in word, neither in tongue; but in deed and in truth." (I. John, iii., 18`„ and in the evening he based his sermon on the passage: " Ye can discern the face of the sky : hut can ye not, discern the signs of the times ?' (Matthew ivi. 3.) The school children occupied seats on a specially- erected gallery, and sang some anniversary hymns very pleasingly. The choir rendered the anthems " Walk about Zion " and " Break forth into joy " (both by Caleb Simper). In the afternoon a flower service was held and a cantata entitled "The flower mission " as very creditably given. The soloists were Miss May Isherwood, Miss May Miller and Miss E. Hughes, and duets were interpreted by Miss Ellison and Miss Dutton. Mr. Quine presided, and the connective readings were given by Mr. it If. Meldrum. Praise is due to Mr. P. E. Penketh, the painstaking conductor, and to Miss E. Miller, who presided at the organ.

"GREAT TALKERS OF OUR TIME." ,INTERESTING LECTURE. On Monday evening the Rev. S. T. Besward delivered his popular lecture on " Great talker of our time " before a fairly large audience. Mr. James Povey, also presided, said Sunday schools had been the salvation of the country. Mr. Raikes little thought what the movement would grow to when he inaugurated it. The Sunday schools were the finest institutions in the lend. Men might squabble abont the Education Bill and go to prison and pat others in prison, but he had no fear so long as they could keep their Sunday schools. The influence of the Sunday school was so far-reaching, nearly all the great men in our country having received their early training there. (Applause.) The Rev. S. T. Bosward began his lecture by inform- ing the audience that although his subject was "Great talkers of our time " he was not going to talk about the ladies. (Laughter.) He would not talk even about the suffragettes. (Laughter.) In spite of the many cheap jokes made at the expense of the ladies' he believed they talked a great deal less than the men. When they considered the enormous amount of talk poured forth by men in Parlia- ment, Town Councils and other institutions, they would see that the talking which the ladies did was very much leas and often a great deal more interesting than that which the men perpetrated. (Laughter.) When he spoke of" great talkers " he did not mean merely those who had done a great 'deal of talking. Many people talked an infinite deaf of nothing. (Laughter.) Yet, after all, quantity must be taken into account and he would not call that man a great talker who merely gave utterance to a few permanent aphorisms. If mere quality were taken into account without reference to quantity, any of us might become great talkers. One of the greatest talkers of tife last century was Samuel Taylor Coleridge. Talk Was his recreation and his busi- ness :it was almost his meat and drink. He talked ail his life long and toward* the close of his life he scarcely did anything else. it was said that be spoke about every subject, frail shoe lelther to the solar system. (Laughter.) To those acho could appreciate hies, the recollection of a conversation with Coleridge was one of the most treasured memories they retained. Another great talker who lived almost in our own times was Lord Macaulay. He was a great Parliamentary orator, and some of the speeches he delivered were so ornate and highly polished that they could scarcely be conceived of as Parliamentary speeches to-day. He had two qualities which gave him his wonderful power as a talker—a memory which never let go a single fact which had once got within its grip, and a marvellous ability for turning thoughts into sr aech. He did more talking than any man of his age. To come to a more recent Hod, the greatest talker of our time was William Ewart Gladstone. (Applause.) He else a man of such brilliant genius, and his career was so remarkable and ',deed so tortuous, and he had Etta a variety of gifts that it was very difficult as yet to form a calm estimate of him. As a talker Gladstone seemed to be altogether unique. He must have delivered in Parliament some 8,003 speeches, and probably three times as many short statements and replies to questions. ro those must be added the speeches he made at railway stations, at public dinners, before learned societies, and to great masses of the public in popular meetings. The quantity of Gladstone's speech Was like a mighty mountain, the image of vastncss, or a perpetual stream which rolled on its channel ever full, and with force resistb-ss and resources boundless. Ife, in fact, did more talking than any man or woman who ever lived. The quality, too, was quite as remarkable :1 the quantity. When ho entered Parliament he was at once recognized as a brilliant talker but it was not till he had passed his fortieth year that he rose to the higheat position as a Parliamentary debater. The lecturer gavo some pemonal reminis- swan of sr sc ahes by Gladstone who, he said, could hold and awe, enthral and charm by the magic of his words. He talked many abuses out of esistence and talked reforms 4-1' • existence. He talked the Nonconformists into the Universities from wh'ch they had bean excluded for so many years, ho talked the Irish Church into freedom, he almost talked the nation into belief in Home Rule, he talked the count' y into a white heat of indignation against the Bulgarian atrocities, and for many years the talking of Gladstone was one of the greatest political forces in England or in Europe. It was said that Benjamin Disraeli was not the greatest man in Parliament but he was the strongest, and if that were so, it was due to that tongue of his—a tongue with which he so frequently stung and inflamed his opponents. He was a prince of debaters,partly because he had complete control of his 014.1 temper but very often through his epigrams which were remembered to this day and were quoted almost daily. Sometimes he became so grandiloquent that he made his friends shiver and his enemies roar. Another rival of Gladstone was Robert Lowe. lie was a man who had a great many disadvantages. His eyesight was so poor that he could not see his notes and his memory was so poor that he could not do without them. (Laughter.) His articula- tion was very imperfect and his manners were awkward; yet he became ono of the greatest debaters in the House and during the 1800 session it was said that he matched and over-matched both Gladstone and Bright when they were at their highest and best. A friendly yet successful vival of Gladstone was the good old Quaker John Bright—(applause)—one of the most honest men who ever entered into the public life of England. Gladstone was a men of iron constitution ; Bright was very delicate. Gladstone was a scholar ; Bright was a man of moderate education. Gladstone was a profound and subtle thinker ; Bright saw things plainly and expressed them simply. It bad been said by good judges that some of Bright's speeches were superior to anything of Gladstono's and the place of supreme ability in oratory had been assigned to Bright. The most remarkable thing about him Was his foresight. He seemed almost to have the gift of prophecy. Many of the things he advocated wore unpopplar in his day but now they were accepted. lie loved righteorsness and maintained the cause oteighteousness with all the resources of his glorious eloquence. He did work which many people would not call religious work, but it was religious because it was done in the religious spirit. Many of the great talkers of our time had bc professedly preachers It must not be supposed that preachers were necessarily ignorant, backward and reactionary r arsons, not understanding the times and their necessities. These were no doubt preachers who were behind the times, whose theology had a musty smell and whose exegesis and argameets were ante- deluvian in character. (Laughter.) Such preachers ought no doubt to be patio some museum of antiquities. (Laughter.) 'have were, however, preachers of a, different type who were fully alive to the re quiremente of the age and whose words were strong and bold. Charles IL Spurgeon was certainly one of the greatest talkers of the age. He was not a polished orator or a great scholar. His th )logy was somewhat out of date, no doubt ; it was somewhat narrow. Yet his wonderful earnestness, his splendid command of pure English, his glorious voice and his enthusiasm made him one of the greatest powers in the nation for many years. Next in cnapacter and ability they must place William Morley Punshon. 'Dee secret of his popularity was not deep thirking, originality or learning. His style was very simple, but he put infinite pairs into his work and had a most astonishing gift of elocutior Above all he Was intensely in earnest. Another gas .t wencher of the last centmy was Joseph Parker. of the City Temple. Some of those present bad no cloud visited the City Temple. He (the lecturer) hoped they did so five years or so ago. There had teen a considerable chs age in the character of the teaching disr :treed from the pelpit of the City Temple within the last few years. Joseph Parker was a man of more genius than Spurgeon or Punsbon. He was peehaps not so popriar as either, but be was unquestionably a man of great originality and eloquence. Hugh Price Hughes, with whom he (the lecturer) was essociatedsiorty years ago, was a piince of debaters. lie had marvellous quickness of thought and ability in retorting upon opponents. His death was the greatest loss the Methodist Cnurch had sustained, and he would long be remembered not only as a debater and preacher, but as one of the most eloquent talkers in public and in private that Methodism had ever pro- dnced. As to some great living talkers, it would be rather invidious to mention names so he would describe one or taco and leave the names to his hearers'judgment. 'moue was one men who a few years ago was certainly one of the most distinguished talkers of our time—a statesman who had been reduced to silence, and none of them could tell whether the silence was temporary or permanent. A few years ago his talk had echoes in at least three Continent, and had a great deal to do in shaping the destinies and fen 'tunes of this empire and of mankind at large. When 'addressing huge audiences be wee always cool and self- possessed, There was no tremor to disturb the orchid in his coat or the monocle from which he calmly gazed on the palpitating throng. There was another man who might be a great talker if he would—a man of various gifts who had played many parts in his time. He was an aristocratic yet a democratic statesman, a breeder of race horses, a writer of books, a man who spent his time partly as a great leader and partly as a recluse and student. Sometimes he came forth like Achilles from his tent and delivered an oration to the people and then many people thought the millennium had come mad looked for better times straight away.

(Laughter.) But they found very soon that he had ietired into his tent or tabernacle once more and he was not seen or heard for a long season. Sometimes be came and urged his friend 4 to devote themselves to spade work—(laughter)—hut he preferrod to plough his lonely furrow. tie called out for efliciency but did not define it or do anything to bring it about.. Let them hope that by and by, even after so long a time he would wake up and take the position for which he time, been so well fitted by Nature and by Providence—the position of one of the greatest talkers of our time. The lecturer concluded by remarking that no gift involved more responsility than that of speech and he urged his hearers to use it to the glory of God and the benefit of their fellow men. (Applause.)
A vote of thank; to the lecturer condoled a success- ful meeting.
An Appeal to Young Man.

The Rev. John Yonge preached a special sermon to young men at Wycliffe Church on Sunday evening, his text being "And Saul said to him, whose son art thou, thou young man? And David rinswered,l ant the son of thy servant Jesse, the Ilethjehemite " (I. Samuel xvii., 53). Ile said it would he a fine and blessed out- come of that service if there could be awakened in the soul of every youth, every young man present th,l greatest of all consciousnes -that he was a son of God. It was very much to be doubted whether any such sublime consciousness did exist in the majority of young men. If it did, surely its influence would be more manifest. Surely there would be more generally seen an infinitely higher and finer type of manhood. urely the long talked of millennium would dawn on the human race, if all mankind could wake up to the universal sense of its divine origin. lie wanted to insist by that address upon the great truth that one of the "greatest Christian doctrines Is the divine origin of human nature. The great Christian message was that which called upon men to claim their birthright and live their life as the sons of God. There was no manhood so true, so fine, so strong, so completely manly as that of" the man in I Christ."

Suffragettes P , - The Rev. IL E. Letheren's subject on Sunday evening at the Baptist Church proved to be an interesting excur- sion into the by-ways of the Bible. It was bused upon the story of " Zelophehad's Daughters " told in sundry passages of the Book of Numbers. In the tribe of Manasseh there had been a man Zelophehad by name who had died in the desert. He had no sons to enter upon his inheritance in Canaan but ,only daughters and no daughter might inherit in her own right. This law seemed to these women to be less than justice and they laid their case before Moses with such results as the story shows. He contrasted the position of women in Israel with that of their sisters in other lands. But though much was theirs they wanted more and their story shows how they made the bounds of freedom wider yet. After hinting at the difference between the method pursued by these women and that adopted by certain of their modern representatives Mr. Letheren proceeded to point the modern lessons of this ancient story. They won the way for others. A new principle of law was raid down which greatly enlarged the liberties of Israel's daughters. A great principle of grace was anticipated that in Christ is neither male nor female but if we are His we are heirs :recording to promise.

of a performance. His method is to give marks, and for choirs his figures arc as follows : (a) Accuracy of Notes and Time. (Hax. 10). (i) Tone, Voice Quality and Production, Intonation, Blend. (Max. 20). (c) Attack, Pronunciation, Enunciation. (Max. If) (d) Expression, Pace, Interpretation. (Max. 20). (r) General Effect. (Max. 20). Some adjudicators object to marks, preferring to trust to the general impression made upon the mind. Dr. McNanght admits he does not require fignres if there are, say, three or four choirs and there is only one test piece. But when there are six or eight choirs, and they have to sing perhaps four pieces (two in the after- noon end two in the evening)) he rightly says it is impossible to carry the effect in the mind without marks. Another excellent qualification in Dr. McNaught is the happy way he gives his decisions. He is always bright, with a touch of humour now nod again. He says exactly what be means, and he mears exactly what he says. He never discourages though ! he may have to find fault. He has the knack of hiding I the pill of criticism in the form of pleasant, jocular speech, and the dose is taken with benefit. Some adjudicators say (unintentionally no doubt) unkind things and criticise so unmercifully that the competi- tors resolve never to try again ; others let their tongues run away with then, and no one is the wiser for their remarks. As .Dr. McNaught says, it is the worst choirs we want to get in these competitions, and the best choirs are there to give the lesson and show how it can be done. Young conductors get new ideas and village choirs especially hear something better than they have heard before. It is therefore the greatest folly for an adjudicator to damp the enthusiasm of any choir, and on that account he should carefully weigh every word he says before giving utterance to it. Referring to the beneficial influence of these competi- tion festivals that are springing up in England, Dr. alcNaught says he is greatly surprised:at the marked improvement in the choirs taking part. . . . Of the , Welsh Eisteddfod Dr. McNaught has mixed feelings. Of the Welshman's love of musiche is thoroughly con- Ninced, but lie thinks their singing lacks breath and repose. Their Eisteddfod arrangements too, are open to improvement and he is hopeful that ere long there will be a distinct advance in the musical life of Wales. Much more might be said about Dr. McNaught and his work, but my space has gone. It is impoisible to estimate what he has done and is doing for the cultiva- tion of music in England. His influence is felt in all parts, and his connection with the Musical Competition Festivals is bound to grow year by year. Long may he be spared to carry on his excellent work.

div.head: WARRINGTON MUSICAL FESTIVAL.
div.p: WARRINGTON MUSICAL FESTIVAL.
THE PRINCE OF ADJUDICATORS."

I The committee of the IVarrington Musical Festival, which takes place at the Parr Hall on Saturday neat, have been fortunate in securing the services of such an eminent adjudicator as Dr. W. G. McNeught. We Ilextract the following from an article by " Broad Nib " published in the April number of " The Musical Journal " under the heading " Master Musicians " : The Prince of Adjudicators " is a term that has been applied to Dr. McNaught on more than one occasion, land it is a description of him that would be very generally endorsed. Undoubtedly he is She adjudicator of the present day, for he possesses in a large degree the many qualifications necessary to be a really success- ful and useful judge in musical competitions; but more lon this subject later on. In the meantime let us trace the career of this well-known gentlenign. William Gray McNaught was born in the East-End of London on March 30th, 1849. When old enough he was sent to a school in the neighbourhood, and it was here that ho first got an insight into music, especialla the tonic sol-fa system. So rapidly did he learn that he soon took his place amongst the altos in some of the large festivals held at the Crystal Palnee. The late Dr. John Kennedy (the highly-esteemed minister of Stepney Meeting) rd his family took a keen interest in the ' youth. A son ef Dr. Kennedy's—now Sir Alexander B. W. Kennedy of engineering fame— studied the violin with him ; after acquiring proficiency they started free classes at various centres for teaching the instrument. On completion of his school education, young MoNaught was placed in an &rice in the City, but all his spare time—and his interest too—were devoted to music. He sought and devoured all the musical litera- ture he could lay his hands on. He was a member of the choir managed by Messrs. Ashoroft and Evans, a well-known East-End choir in those days, and he con- ducted a band connected with it. Ills connection with the late Mr. Andrew Ashcroft was very helpful, for that well-informed amateur pushed the youth on and gave him as much musical work as he could. Observing his enthusiasm , and his thoroughness, he later on advised him to go into the musical profession. Even at this time ho conducted oratorio performances at various places, and on one occasion at least he not only con- ducted a cantata, but also took the bass solos ! For a time young McNaught was the late Rev. John Curwen's amanuensis, and assisted him in the prepara- tion of his works on tonic sol-fa. Probably this experi- ence to a large extent paved the way to his work in connection with school music in later life. His commercial career was short, as in 1871 he " retired from business "and immediately- went to the Royal Academy of Music, where he studied harmony under the late Sir G. A. Macfarren, violin under Mr. William Foulkes, singing under Mr. F. R. Cox, and pianoforte under the late Mr. Thomas Wingharn. Amongst his fellow-students were Eaton Parking, Frederic Corder, L. N. Parker, W. Frye Parker, and last, but not least, Edward German. While we:king , at the Academy (where he remained till MG) he was ' busy in other directions. He had a large choir at Stepney, and in July, 1873, they won a prize at the National Musical Meetings held at the Crystal Palace in those days, the judges being Messrs. Barnby, Henry Leslie, and J. Benedict. He also was appointed pre- centor at Stepney Meeting, a position he 'held for ten 1 years. But probably his best work at this time was in coracltion xi,:th the Bow and Bromley I institute, where in 1874 he was appointed conductor of the choir rid orchestra and teacher of the music classes. Many excellent oratorio performances were given during his sixteen years' reign. How much Dr. McNaught did for music at the East-End of London through the Bow and Bromley Institute will never be knov.a. IPs resignation was a source of the greatest regret in the district, and in token of the regard felt for him a presentation was made in December, 1900. What Dr. MoNaught does not know about school music and musical teaching in schools ia not worth knowing. He has read pretty well everything that has lsen written on the subject ; he has travelled at home and abroad to study the methods under different rules and circumstances. As a teacher he is excellent, and he never fails to secure the close attention and the admira- tion of all attending his school classes. His happy manner would soon subdue the most obstinate pupil. 'Lee year ISB3 was an important one in Dr. MeNangbt's life, for he was then appointed by the late Sir John Stainer as one of his Assistant Inspectors of Music 51 the Education Department. Naturally his previous experience eminently qualified him to fill such an important post, and his discharge of the duties was in every way most satisfactory. To estimate how many children _passed through his hands would be quite . . .

7 impossible, but he examined individually at least 26,000 teachers. In IS9O he received from the Archbishop of Canterbury the degree of Doctor of Music, through the instrumentality of Sir George Grove and Sir John Stainer, exerted without Dr. McNaught's knowledge. In 1901 Sir John Stainer died. He had been

;n failing health for some time, and Dr. McNaught had latterly done all the work. Naturally everyone interested in school music thought that Dr. MeNaught would be promoted to Stainer's position. He had certainly earned the right to it, and his qualifications were rndoubted.- More than that, there was no man living who could claim to have anything like the same know- ledge and experience. To the astonishment of the educational world, however, he was passed over and the appointment given to a comparatively unknown man. Much sympathy was felt and expressed for Dr. McNaught, because his life bad, in recent years at least, been shaped for such a position. He, however, has the satisfaction of knowing that his excellent work has greatly influenced the musical life of the country, and the fruit of his labour will remain. Although the action of the Education Department in not appointing Dr. McNaught as Inspector was a severe and keen disappointment to all interested in music, as things have turned out, possibly it has upon the whole been a gain to the cultivation of musical education in England. Without in any way seeking it, work RS a musical adjudicator came at once to Dr. McNaught, and so eminently is be fitted for that position Viet the calls upon him in that direction have increased rapidly, and to-day he has far more engagements of the kind than any other man. Last year no less than 403 choirs passed through his hands, and this year that number will be considerably increased. Even now be has eighty days booked for adjudications; from Eater Monday to the end of June he has very few vacant dates, and his work will take him to all parts of England, and occasionally to Scotland and Ireland. I sin not surprised, for he possesses gifts that make him admirably fitted for the duties ' • for be is an excellent judge, and can detect instantly the good and bad poinf;

Do not thrtw away burnt boiled milk, but pour it into a jug, and put this into a basin of cold water, leaving it until the milk is lukewarm. The burnt tast n will then have disappeared. • ‘N
To clean the pipe of the scullery sink ndd a teaspoonful of powdered ammonia to two tablespoonfuls of soda, and pour over it a gal- lon of boiling water. This will dissolve any grease in the sink.
To avoid breakaacs when washing glass, fold a towel sevsral times and place it in the bottom of the bowl used for washing up. This prevents thin glass from breaking and chip- ping.

Rom' an Pie.—Line a pie-dish or mould with short paste, then fill with layers of nicely boiled macaroni, thin slices of cooked veal or other white meat, grated Parmesan cheese, a little cayenne pepper, salt, and finely-chopped onion. Pour in sufficient cream or milk to moisten the whole. Cover with short crust and bake thoroughly. Serve when cold, turned out of the mould.

To cleatise brass 'pans that have not been used for some time, scour with salt and vine- gar to remove any sign of verdigris. Clean with a -good polishing paste, then rinse out with plenty of hot water, and dry with Loft cloths. After treating brass and copper pans like this they can be used for any kind of cookery.

French Rice Pudding.—Take two ounces rice, one pint milk, one ounce butter, cinna- mon, two eggs, two tablespoonfuls sugar. Boil the rice in the milk for half an hour till quite 'tender • when taken off the fire add the butter and let it cool ; flavour with cinna- mon. put the flavoured rice into a pie-dish, stir in the well-beaten yolks of two eggs and sugar; heat the Whites of the eggs to a stiff froth, and mix it with the • other ingredients and bake in a moderate • oven until a golden brown.

Here is ,a good way to curl black tips of feathers : Take the feather in left hand, out- side tip, and pass one 'dozen or .so of the strands flat over the end of the thumb, say an inch or more over the thumb, or according to the depth required, and with the blunt. side of an old knife, draw the, strands across it, from the point of the thumb, towards you. Continue until the whole feather is done, and it will look as good as new. When a feather has been damp, it can be " successfully re- curled by sprinkling some rought salt on it, and shaking it before a good fire.

A wash for sunburn and heat-rash is what many of us need during hot weather, and the lotion prescribed here will be found bcnefl- cail in the alleviation of heat-rash and of the irritation caused by exposure to the sun: Take of simple tincture of benzoin one drachm, boric acid 10 gains: glycerine two drachms, elder flower water six ounces. Place these in a bottle, and shake it well till the boric acid is quite dissolved. Apply to the skin with a piece of cotton wool.

Fruit and natter Pudding,—To half a pound of flour allow one pint of milk, poured in a little at a time, stirring briskly ; add one ounce sugar and a little ground ginger or nutmeg, and a well-beaten egg. Put equal quantities of batter and any kind of fruit, such as black or red currants, gooseberries, damsons, plums, etc., or apples cut in quar- ters. Sprinkle thickly with sugar, and boil in a basin, or bake in a quick oven for hours. If apples are used they must be a sort that cook quickly.

When washing milk dishes, such as cans, pails, churn, and so on, always wash first in tepid water, and then scald with jot water. If washed in hot water first, the milk will coagulate and adhere to the vessels, and if left -to dry will taint the milk and butter. "A new broom sweeps clean," and if when the new broom is bought, a picture-frame screw with ring) is put in the end of the handle, and the broom hung up when not in use, it will "sweep clean' much • longer. Try this, friends—it IS "true economy."

Some persons like a soapy preparation for cleaning the teeth, and when slightly per- fumed it lends an agreeable odour to the breath. A preparation of this kind can be made of white castile soap powdered two drachms, recti&ed alcohol six drachms, oil of geranium four drops, tincture, of red sandal wood two drachms, water two ounces. Dis- solve the soap in the spirit, add the oil and tincture and finally the water. Sprinkle a few drops on the toothbrush, and use with %Tater.' • .

Good Tomato Sau'eq.—This is always ap- preciated with boiled cauliflower, macaroni, fowl, or fish. Take eight ripe tomatoes, cut them •up, skins and all, and stew till they are very soft, then press through a sieve, sea- son highly with salt and cayenne pepper. Add • a gill of thick brown gravy and heat, stirring till the sauce boils. Serve at once.

A very good temporary stopping for a leak In either a gas or water pipe may be pro- duced by working powdered whiting and yel- low soap into a paste. Press it into the leak- ing part of the pipe, and put on sufficient to make file hole airtight. This is only a tem- porary remedy, and should not prevent the plumber being secured at the first possible moment.

Olive oil, though incapiae of supporting life if taken alone, nevertheless, writes a well-known physician, lends itself to a di- minished meat diet, as it prevents waste of tissue elements, and thus renders less neces- sary a meat or proteid diet, which would otherwise be increased and harmful. It tends to promote all digestive processes, and keeps human fat at a normal standard of composi- tion. And as fat is the food of the skin, it follows that the more pure and perfect the food the better the condition of the skin. The warm, rosy complexion of the Italian and Sicilian women as due to the -free use of olive oil as much as to the air and climate of their country. From one or two tablespoon- fuls of olive oil' spread over the day ia iff- L'eut ways is quite sufficient.
