div.head: WARRINGTON FOOTBALL
div.p: WARRINGTON FOOTBALL
CLUB.
ANNUAL REPORTS.

The annual meeting of the Warrington Football Club, will be held on Thursday nest at the Ca-operative Hall, Cairo-street. The following are the Secretary's and Treasorer's reports and other business : SECRETARY'S REPORT.

Mr. H. Ashton (hon. secretary) reports to the mem- bers as follow : "The past season has been one of eventualities, the most striking being the advent of a professional organization from New Zealand playing under the auspices of the Northern Union and thus con- founding the statement of Mr. Wray Palliser and his Rtietry Union friends that the professional "All Black " combination was a phantom one. The accession of the Ebbw Vale and Merthyr Clubs to our Union was a con- vincing proof that the interest in our game was on the increase in a most gratifying and satisfactory manner. Both clubs have had a very fair season financially, and the founders are sttisfled with the results. The Inter- national match in Wales was of itself a remarkable event. Besides being very well patronised, the spectators epoke enthusiastically of the game, and the "Western Mail," "Argus,"and other leading Welsh papers described it as one of dazzling brilliancy. Additional test matches were played, one taking place ,in the Metropolis—for the first time in the history of the Northern Union—on the ground of the Chelsea Club. The game proved a most attractive and interesting one, I the' London press paying it a very great compliment. Their reports described the game as scientific es well as I particularly interesting. The first team of your Club have played 37 matches won 23, lost 11, and drawo 3. Training operations com- menced early in good earnest. A small charge for admission was made for the first time, the proceeds being devoted to charitable purposes. Indications were conveyed to your committee that the form displayed by the players during the practice matches of their fitness, and it was generally felt, with the quality of the material on hand,the season's prospects were promising. The early matches justified such hopes, as Leigh, Roch- dale, and Runcorn were defeated in turn. The defeat at St. Helens was a great disappointment, attached to which was practically the 1, as of the S.W.L. Cup. Oldham, our only loss at home, was also an unfortunate slip. Losing Tilley at an early period of the game mitigated materially against our chances of success. Runcorn, in the first round of the Lancashire Cup, were met and defeated ; then followed a reverse at Leigh in the second round,after a hard game,by 13 points to 11. A sequence of wins followed, and a very flue game at Ebhw Vale was characterized by local critics as the best exhibition ever shown in South Wales. Broughton beat us .at Wheater's Field, then away to Oldham, which proved a very stubborn and exciting match. -The visit of the " All Blacks " was a very- eventful one. Unfortunately the day opened wet, the ground in consequence being on the hefts/ side. How- ever, after a spirited contest we won by 8 points to 7. Beating L _sigh away on Christmas Day, then Widnes at home, we journeyed to Hull only to experience another misfortune, as besides a beating, we lost that clever half back, S. Lees, who sustained a broken collar bone, A loss to Runcorn away also followed, then Barrow, Swinton and Broughton were handeomely beaten in turn. A most unsatisfactory period next ensued, the outcome of which practically destroyed all our hopes of entering the first four of the League. We only recorded 1 point out of a pessible 8 at this stage. A vast improvement was- shonn in the return Wigan match, which created anticipations of a most optimistic character seeing the Cup-ties were on band. Our old opponents Halifax were drawn to oppose us in the first round of the N.C. Cup. a stiff task certainly, but which was accomplished successfully after a very exciting contest. Bradford end Hull each net with a reverce at Wilderspool,tben we encountered Runcorn for the fourth time this season in the second round for the Cup. A splendid win for us entitled us to enter the last S. The luck of the draw went to Broughton thus once more caking us to necomplish a big task. This it is believed by many would have I:en nchieved, bat for serious disaster in first few minutes of the game as F. Jenkins, one of the festest and cleverest forwards we have,was damaged so seriously that he was of no further use. Tilley also was unable to turn out for this match. St. Helens, then Leeds on Good Friday, a Success in each, brought our League programme to a conclusion. An invitation ns Cap -holders u-as extended to us to contest en exhibition in London with another notable N.U. team and nccepted. We met Wakefield Trinity at West Ham. Neither the result nor the display of our players wee very creditable,but from all accornts the state of the ground was against spirited play. The "A "Team have played 28 matcher, won 23 end lost 5. Except the away match at linnecno, generally speaking the " A " teem have performed fairly satis- factorily until they encountered Wigan " A " on one ground in a Combination fixture. In this match,they were rather easily beaten which to all intents destroyed all hopes of their winning the Championship. Further misfortune descended upon them when through frost and other causes the fixtures with Wigan " A," Salford, Pemberton, Leigh Shamrocks and Wigan Highfield hid to be postpened, the Clubs taking only one point each. The Shield Competition on the Knock-out principle was instituted for "A " teams end juniors end proved an unqoalified success, doing a great amount of good for the juniors. Our men finished second in the Com- bination, and contested the Finn 1 Shield-tie with Wigan " A " in the presence of a huge crowd at Wignn, a .gat of £l3B being taken. The result was is disappointing wind-up to onr season, as Wigan " A " beat the War- rington men by 19 points to 6, and thus became first holders of the Shield.

Daring the season great difriculties were encountered by the varied and numerors injuries to players. On several occasions our resources were seriously taxed to place anything like a representative team in the field, and this to no measured degree was the primary cause of the first team's dovcnfall. Practically at various periods during the season, almost every playing member has been incapacitated and this to my intelligent observer is a very great disadvantage to any team. The Works Medal Competition has once more teen successful and although the receipts have not aggregated as much as last season yet on the whole, results have been gratifying ,considering the wretched wei.ther experienc?d almost throughout the competition. Several likely juniors have been invited to sign and they have signified their desire to do so. Your President has taken a very deep interest in the management of your Ciub end has attended a great many meetings. Your Committee also have discharged their arduous duties very ably and attentively." TREASURER'S REFORT.

Mr. T. Pemberton (hon. treasurer) reports as follows :—" Herewith I beg to submit for your approval the accounts of the past season. The member- ship now amounts to 1,071 against 920 at the end of sesson 1906-7. The receipts at the gates have been corsiderably less than those for the season 1906-7, and the rayments to other Clubs have been larger, the net gate being £l,BlO 10s. 10d. against £2,299 HA. large number of accidents that have occurred caused a ercat number of claims to be made on the Insmanco Company. The payments to doctors specialists, and Nursing Homes have been very heavy, increased £3l 2s. 6d., and I regret to say that three of our players are still prevented from working owing to injuries. The expenses in connection with D. Isherwood's Benefit amounted to £25 18s. Bd., enabling this player to receive a balance of £165 10s. 4d. The journey to London to play Wakefield cost the Club £lB Cs. ld, the expenses being £25 12s. Bd. less our share of the gate from the London Northern Union Club £7 4s. id. A considerable amount of money has been expended in obreining new players. WonKs COM PETITION.—The amount at the disposal of the Committee is £69 3s. 6d. and out of this there has been granted to the Infirmary Extension Fund £2O, Infirmary Revenue Fund £2O, Nurses' Institution 12 guineas, St. John's Ambulance Society £6, and compensation Hs been pad to players hr-t 4're Competition.

div.head: NOTES ON GAMES AND ATHLETICS.
div.p: NOTES ON GAMES AND ATHLETICS.
Cricket.

Two Nuccessive defeats cannot be regarded as a. very promising opening of the season so far as Warrington is concerned. There is, however,, this much in Warrington's favour— that Ashton-under-Lyne, by whom they were severely trounced on Saturday, are about the strongest eleven they will have to meet this reason, and the ‘Varring- : touinns took the field with a somewhat weak team. I Ashton had first turn with the bat, and such a magnifi- cent stand did three of their players make that the I innings was declared at 173 for 4. Whitehead piled on : sixty runs for Ashton and then carried out his bat, his hitsincluding eight 4's. G.liatcliffe was not far behind, knocking up 54 in dashing style, and being caught and bowled by Podmore S. E. Eaton added 39. -- Warrington had little hope of winning the match, . and a very poor start was made, for off the third ball Isent down by Huish J. Callon drove one into the hands 1 of N.S.Eaton at mid-off. W.Richardson showed a sound , defence, but W. H. Podmore, after placing one to the leg boundary, made a mishit and was easily caught by 10. L. Eaton. T. Wright failed to negotiate a fast yorker from Whitehead, so that three good wickets were down for eleven runs. Cresswell joined, Richard- son and helped to stop the rot, the majority of the runs coming from the professional's bat. At 25 the young • amateur spooned one into the bands of mid-on. B. Silcock came next and a prolonged stay was made until S. L. Eaton took the ball from Whitehead and off the ' first delivery Cresswell was well held at the wicket. Ho had made an excellent 29. Three runs later both H. Dolan and B. Silcock left, and from this period the howlers had the upper hand. finish bowled with deadly effect and captured 5 wickets for 23 runs. The Warring- ton innings closed for 72.

The second eleven are doing better than their sZniors ' and on Saturday registered their second victory, at the expense of Ashton-under-Lyne at Arpley. Thn visitors battvd first, but, with the exception of Wright, NA ho made they were helpless against the deliveries of Bennett who accounted for seven wickets for 24 runs. The innings only resulted in an aggrerate of 57, and against this %Varrington put together 81 for the loss of seven wickets, S. Partridge playing brilliantly for his 34.

div.head: LORD MORLEY'S BATTLE OF LIFE.
div.p: LORD MORLEY'S BATTLE OF LIFE.

Lord Morley of Blackburn, replying to the letter of congratulation from the Blackburn Town Council, says they " will readily understand how much I must be moved by these words of salutation from the great town whence L went out long years ago to fight the battle of life. I prize such recognition, though only too well aware of my thousand shortcomings below its standard."

There were some interesting

CONDITIONS and important speeches at OF COMPROMISE the meeting of the Congre- gational Union on Tuesday. That of Dr. JOHN MASSIE, M.P., was only of less immediate consequence than that of D. GUINNESS ROGERS. Both had reference to the Education Bill which is to come up for second reading in the House of Commons next Monday. It has been stated in many quarters of late, with a great amount of confidence, that the Bill is to be dropped—under certain conditions. Sioull the intended conference be satisfaltory, we shall have a new Bill next year, based upon its decisions. In the meantime there is to be no backing down, and even the conference cannot take plac3 until the principle of the Bill has 1333 n affirmed on second reading. Dr. MASSIE is clearly o! opinion that nothing great is to be expected as a result of the present talk about compromise. His views are evidently founded on the basis of CANNrso's famois rhyming despatch to the AMBASSADOR at the Hague:

"The fault of the Dutch Is giving too little - And asking too much." There is, said De. MAssrE, an unc;nscious unreality about the proposals that are being made. Dr. GUINESS ROGERS endorsed this expressiOn of opinion by saying that " they could not submit to Lord HALIFAX." That is the situation in a nut- shell. There can be no compromise with Lord HALIFAX, because that nobleman will be content with nothing but surrender. He and two or three others (four of them altogether, in fact) were responsible for the worst features of Mr. BALFOUR' s Act. There was Lord HALIFAX, there was Lord HUGH CECIL, there was the BISHOP Of SOUTHWARK, and there was the Bishop of Southwark's brother, Mr. TALBOT. They had a tremendous scheme for putting the little Nonconformist in the Church of England mill, grinding him up ansonp,, ecclesiastical formulas, and turning him out as a little member of the Establishment.

If this had not been the case, we should have been spared several years of religious warfare within the political arena. Certainly there can be no compromise with Lord Ilmirax. The special views of those who are of his way of thinking have nothing to do with the education question. They are perfectly entitled to hold them. We have never refused to admit their sincerity and earnest- ness, and to accord them the respect which is the due of sincerity and earnestness. Nobody wants to interfere in the domestic arrangements of the Church ; the whole Eras- tian creed is obnoxious to us ; we desire to see it abolished. But, on the other hand, Lord HALIFAX and his friends should have no special voice, save as citizens on terms of equality with other citizens, in civic affairs. Ic is more than ridiculous that they should be permitted to stand in the way of a great educational settle- ment. This country is behind all the leading civilisations, very far indeed behind its own Colonies and the United States, in r3spect of the education of its- youth. What keeps it so far in the rear is the religious difficulty, which really resolves itself into a question as to whether the path of progress is to be obstrusted by Lord HALIFAX.
Dundee has done what Manchester_ regrets its

div.head: STAUNCH SCOTS.
div.p: STAUNCH SCOTS.

- . failure to do—in returning Mr. Winston Churchill to the House of Commons by a huge majority. Manchester was decidedly Peckhamised on the eventful day, with the result that the opportunity for securing the President of the Board of Trade as its representative was lost for ever. The Scots of Dundee proved them- selves less liable to political frolicksomeness, and in the course of one short week made up their minds that Churchill was the man for them. They were not deluded by the trashy appeals of the Tariff Reformers, the Brewers, and the Coal Con. sumers, or scared out of their wits by the militant bell-clanging suffragettes. There is a staunchness about Scottish political conviction which takes a lot of upsetting and there was never any doubt about Mr. Churchill receiving from Dundee the ratifica- tion of the Government's great reforming pro- gramme which he desired. The only question was as to whether his majority would be emphatic enough. A lead of 2,709 over his nearest opponent satisfied the most optimistic. Looking at the plain facts and figures of this election we see that Mr. Churchill has raised the Liberal majority to a point which it never reached before 1906, not- withstanding that he bad on his flank a Labour candidate and an advanced teetotal nominee. According to Saturday's polling there is an anti- Tory and Free Trade majority of 11,748 to 4,370 in Dundee. Sir George Baxter, the Conservative and "runner-up," has done Vora() by about 1,000 votes than previous Unionist candidates, who had not the inestimable advantages of a Tariff Reform policy. Even Labour, which returns a representa- tive for Dundee, sustained a most unmistakable set-back by losing nearly 3,000 votes since 1906, thus showing conclusively that Labour cannot hope to succeed without Liberal support. Montrose Burghs election on Tuesday turaed out to be a complete Tory downfall. Mr. R. V. Harcourt (L) polled 3,083 votes, Mr. J. Burgess (Labour) 1,937, and Mr. A. H. B. Constable (C) 1,676. The latter figure represents the smallest Conservative poll in the constituency since 1886. Truly, Toryism and Tariff Reform are in a bad way. The total Free Trade vote divided between the winning Liberal candidate and the Labour candidate exceeds 5,000, and is higher by 600 than the Free Trade vote given solidly to Lord Morleyl In 1906. That Mr. Harcourt, an Englishman unknown to the division, could spare nearly 2,000 Free Trade votes to another Progressive candidate and yet poll almost twice as many votes as the

Conservative is an inspiriting sign not merely of the unshaken soundness of Scottish Liberal opinion but, as we hope, of a fresh current of public opinion in the Liberal direction throughout Great Britain.

We hope the present genera- S EFFIELD'S ton of Warringtonians will PICrURE3. take full advantage of the opportunity now afforded them of seeing a representative exhibition of the work done in charcoal, oil, water-colonr, and sepia, by that gifted man, the late George S'let&ld. He had many associations with Warrington, and nowhere probably was his work more warmly admired. Sixteen years have passed since Sheffield " Mounted the wings of the wind, To go painting among the stars," hot be is still well remembered by many old Warrin,gtonians. As frequently happens in the history of artists and their work, Sheffield's reputation has grown since his death, and the remarkable genius of the man was never so widely recognised as it is to-day. People who possess choice examples of his astonishingly varied work prize them greatly and are only troubled by the difficulty of getting others. The loan exhibi- tion—opened in a speech of such facile expression and intimate knowledge of the artist by Mr. A. H. Crosfield, M.P.—gives an admirable idea of the nature of Sheffield's talents, and his wonderful industry. Those people who neglect to visit the Museum between now andyune Gth, will miss an artistic feast.

Warrington has now an OUR VETERANS. opportunity of doing its duty by those gallant local veterans- who served in the Crimea and Indian Mutiny and other famous campaigns, for a move- ment has been set on foot to raise sufficient funds to ensure that the men who served their country so nobly in days gone by shall spend the rest of their lives in comfort and independence. A strong local sub-committee has been formed, headed by the Mayor (Alderman Smethurst), and an appeal for subscriptions is being issued. Lord Roberts' object in founding the Veterans' Relief Fund was (a) to release from the Workhouses throughout the country those veterans who served in the Critnea and Indian Mutiny, or any previous campaign; (h) to decently pro- vide for them till the end of their days, and (c) to add such a sum to the pensions of all other veterans in poverty as may be thought sufficient. Warrington has been attached to the West Lancashire District, the Chairman of the Committee being the Lord Mayor of Liverpool, and at his request the Mayor hag formed the local Sub-Committee. Inquiries have been set on foot and it has been ascertained that there are eighteen veterans residing in, or in the neighbourhood of Warrington, two being in the Workhouse. "The object of this appeal," says the Mayor, "will, fain sure, meet with the support of all patriots, and I confidently rely on your generosity to enable the Committee to provide for the veterans residing in and near Warrington. The sum required for the purpose will, it is believed, be between £BO and £lOO per annum, and this, I am sure, can be readily raised, as the town and district have always been to the forefrontin supporting any cause which is deserving." We heartily endorse the Mayor's words and hope that the appeal will meet with a ready and substantial response. The ladies, under the leadership of the Mayoress, are also making an effort to raise a worthy contribution from War- rington to the great national fête and bazaar at Chelsea which Lord Roberts has arranged, and their labours, too, should meet with success.

We are glad to notice that MR, BRIM'S Mr. Burns's Housing and BILL. Town-Planning Bill, which should go a long way toward the creation of the City Beautiful, passed its second reading on Tuesday. There was really ro serious opposition to the measure which—unlike most Government Bills—met with the cordial support of all parties, as being designed to prevent a repetition of the enormities which have resulted from the lack of system in the building of towns in the past. The member who discussed the measure with the fullest knowledge of its bearing upon the actual conditions that prevail in England was Mr. Henry Vivian who is well-known to War- rington Liberals and is elways to the forefront in progressive movements. There is no need to emphasise the need for the better housing of the poor, but if there were, Mr. Vivian's demonstra- tion that in Glasgow better housing brings improved physique, and in Edinburgh the line at which the tendency to drunkenness shows a marked increase begins at the line of bad housing, would be con- vincing. Mr. Vivian would like to see more efficient inspection of houses, and this he thinks is , to he secured by having inspectors subject to a central instead of a local authority. Like other far-seeing members, Mr. Vivian finds the town- planning portion of the Bill the most promising of good results. He also wants a little commonsense encouragement for people who are willing and desirous of improving the sanitary and the reithetic conditions of urban life, and with the idea of forestalling the land speculator and the jorry- builder that is embodied in the Bill he is in thorough sympathy.

div.head: BESSES O'TH' BARN BAND. Concerts at the Hippodrome.
div.p: BESSES O'TH' BARN BAND. Concerts at the Hippodrome.

On Sunday the world-famous Besses o'th' Barn Brass Band gave two concerts in the Palace Theatre and Hippodrome. The audiences were not so large as might have been expected but then it should be remembered there were the a/ fresco attractions of an ideal day in early summer tending to keep the public out of doors. But for such as were disposed to make the necessary sacrifice there was a fine musical treat in store in the two programmes which the band played through in its own inimitable style. A. tour round the world and the feteing and pampering of impulsively delighted foreigners have not spoiled the splendid quattities of the bandsmen either individually or collectively. Nor have they affected the absolute sway which Mr. Alec Owen holds over the combined instrumentalists. Many old favourites were played with just the old pointed precision in the attack,the same wonderful restraint in pianissimos and the same magni- ficent volume of tone in the fortes and the grand ensembles. One can but admire the flexibility of cornet in delicate feathery passages fitted only for violins in the "Zauipa " and "II Barbiere " overtures and one wonders how so near an approximation to the com- poser's meaning is made possible. Little bits like that from the " Casse Noisette" suite also teem with difficul- ties for transciiption from stringed to brass instru- ments, yet the " effect" is conveyed in a surprisingly realistic way. Amongst lighter fare such as songs and hymns there were the usual substantial dishes offered us in the shape of selections from Beethoven, from Spohr, and from works like Mendelssohn's " Elijah" all of which serve so well to show the band's strong points. As to the solos, we heard on Sunday some pieces for the euphonium and the trombone which while they were appalling in the exactions made upon the performers and to that extent beyond all praise,sre not altogether free from the objection that to the listener they are not sources of unalloyed pleasure. There was, of course, some enthusiastic and well - deserved acclammation and two encores were responded to. In the evening the band played by special request the beautiful and favourite hymn "Lead kindly light."

Warrington Cycling Club. 1 The May-day festival at Runcorn, the proceeds of which were in aid of deserving local charities, attracted about 20 members of the Warrington Cycling Club on Saturday last. The ride, although somewhat lacking in mileage was voted a complete success,s most enjoyable time being spent in witnessing this old English ceremony. The vagaries of the weather caused an abandonment of the mid-week run on Tuesday evening, the rain descending in torrents as the time of starting approached. However, ample amends were made on Wednesday evening, when about 30 members assembled at the Chapel House, Sankey, the occasion being the opening of the bowling season (the green being reserved for the use of the members on Wednesday evenings). To-day the Club are due at Hale, and given favourable weather a record attendance is expected at this ever-popular resort.

Colonel Hall Walker, M.P., says" the honest public. house is not responsible for drunkenness." There are pablic-houses other than honest then. We should like to ask under which category the tied-houses com; ? It is a pity that Councillor Pemberton's proposal far four ne .v‘ municipal bowling greens was not adopted earlier in the year. There is no sign of the nem greens yet, but the one in Victoria Park, Latchford, is black with bowlers every evening, and most after- noons. Such healthy recreative facilities do a lot in the way of lessening the drink evil. * * Mr. Winston Churchill, on taking the oath yesterday when re-introduced to the House of Cimmons as mem- ber for Dundee' did not, as is usual, kiss the cover of the Testament, but opened the volume and kissed one cf its leaves. The new departure was observed with interest, and members speculated as to whether Mr. Churchill had become apprehensive of the microbic dangers supposed to attend the kissing of the dust- lodged Testaments commonly used in the administering of oaths. . .

* * * Though no delay was admitted in respect of the street repairs at Market-gate, the pin-pricks of the critics seem to have acted as an effective goad on the Paving and Sewerage Committee. This week has seen gigantic efforts put forth on the east side of the street, and the progress made is remarkable. Nearly as much work has been done in six days and nights as took nearly a month to accomplish on the other side. The paviours are showing what they can do tvhen they really try. * * * It did not add to the dignity of Mr. J. C. Parr, D.L. of Grappenball Heyes, when he appeared at the Daresbury Petty Sessions to prosecute the Rev. Sidney Pitt, because the minister's dog had chased a few of the millionaire's sheep. The evidence showed that the dog had been taken for a walk by one of Mr. Pitt's daughters, and feeling the Spring in the air it had apparently rushed among the sheep for a gambol in sheer exuberance of spirits. The sheep fled. Mr. Parr fumed and summoned, and the poor parson paid.

* The annual meeting of *the 1071 memrers of the Warrington Football Club is to be held next Thursday erening,and a harmonious gathering may be expected. The Secretary's and Treasurer's reports are of a satis- factory character on the whole. No football honours have been gained this season, but though the revenue has decreased considerably economic management has resulted in the Club finishing the season with a lose of only £ll on the year's working. The assets —mainly irl cash and investments —am-sant to A:1,511 10s. 5d., and the liabilities to only ..-c_;o3 4s. * * ro Warrington Liberals will* sincerely sympathise with • Mr. Francis Neilson in his failure to win the North §hropshire election on Thursday. After running the late Colonel Kenyon-Slaney so close at the general election he was thought to have a good chance in this bY-election. The Newport Division has, however, remained true to Toryism ever since 1835, and is still unconverted. Mr. Neilson, who helped Mr. Crosfield win here, has made a gallant struggle and may get his reward in some more progressive constituency. * * * Mr. Fred Maddison, N.LP who has often addressed Warrington with great acceptance, has been helping Mr. Francis Neilson in his candidature in Newport !:livision and has had plenty of opportunities of show- Ing his smartness at repartee. He was addressing one meeting when he was interrupted by one of the squires. " You appear from your clothes to be a gentleman," said Mr. Maddison. " I am," was the reply. " Then prove it," said Mr. Maddison ; "gentle- men do not interrupt public speakers when they are putting their views before the people." The rebuke had a good effect, and the popular member for Burnley had a fair bearing.

- swifts are with us at last. It is true that one swallow does not make a summer, but the arrival of the swift betokens the fact that the tale of our summer visitors is complete. Other migrant birds may Yenture to our shores while the skies are wintry and Insect-life scant. Not so the swift. Moving up by degrees from the Cape of Good Hope to Northern gypt, he liugers by the coasts of the Mediterranean till assured of a welco ne in his British nesting- quarters. With his inwers of flight the journey through Spain and France is brief. The southerly Winds at the end of April brought back the swallows and martins in considerable numbers. Tree-pipit, turtle-clove, red-backed shrike, and flycatcher have all In-aPPeared in their accustomed haunts during the past Week. *4* pity the poor brewer ! The Examiner, Saturday, May 16,1908.

Rummage Sale. In connection with St. James' Church a rummage sale was held in the School, Old-road, on Saturday afternoon. The arrangements had been made by the churchwardens, and the sale was a great success. There were a large number of visitors throughout the afternoon and evening, and the stock was welt cleared. The Leather Trade. " The Leather Trades' Review " dealing with the leather trade in Warrington,says : —Since the holidays trade has been disappointing. Contrary to expecta- tion, there has been but little recovery, and everything is very quiet. Some slight improvement is certainly visible, but it is confined to one or t.vo lines, and business generally is of a spasmodic or retail character. Undoubtedly the feature acting most detrimentally to any expansion is the great uncertainty prevailing as to the c urse prices are likely to take. The Infirmary and Dispensary. The Hon. Secretary to the Workingmen's Committee begs to acknowledge, with thanks, the sum of £2O, received from the Warrington Football Club.—The Hon. Treasurer of the institution also acknowledges, with thanks, a donation of £1 10s. received from the Warrington Branch Amalgamated Musicians' Union, through their local secretary, Mr. F. Davies. TRY GILLETTE SAFETY RAZORS for comfort in shaving.—Agent, J. S. GARLAND, 51-55, 13ridge- street:Warrington.—Advt. Unknown Man Poisoned. Coroner Brighouse held an inquest._ at the Swan Hotel, Winwick, on Monday, concerning the death of an unknown man about 2S years of age.—The evidence itowed that deceased was found lying near a stack at Mainfield Farm in an unconscious state, with a small empty bottle by his side. Medical aid was procured but the man died, —Dr. Forrester stated that the empty bottle had contained laudanum. In his opinion the man died from opium poisoning.—P.C. Butler, Croft, said he searched the body and found a note book containing the words written in pencil 'There is no one to blame, and may the Lord bless all my family." —The jury ieturned a verdict that the man died from opium poisoning, there being no evidence to show how it was administered. ASHLEY'S New, Address 4, Buttermarket Street.—Adv

The New Post Office. The date fixed for the opening of the new Post Office is Thursday the 23rd July. The Post Master- General (Right Hon. Sydney Buxton, M.P.), w ill perform the ceremony. Mr. A. H.Crosffield 11.P.will be present. The Irish Vote.

A representative meeting of the Warrington Branch of the United Irish League was held on Monday even- ing at Raddon Court. Mr. John Magian, J.P. (presi- dent), occupied the chair. After conducting the local business, an interesting discussion followed on the recent manifesto of the Irish Party respecting the Irish vote in the English constituencies. It was resolved that the following resolution be forwarded to the chairman of the party : " The Warrington Branch United Irish League of Great Britain wish to express perfect confidence in the attitude recently outlined by the Irish Executive with regard to the Irish electors in Great Britain." PUBLIC BENEFIT—UNDER THE CLOCK FOR BEST BOOTS IN LANCASHIRE.—Advt.

Too Far to Walk. At the Borough Police Court on Saturday Thomas Jones and Frederick Simpson, who hail from Sheffield, were charged with travelling from Liverpool to Warrington on the Cheshire Lines Railway without paying their fares and with intent to avoid payment on Friday at 0 30.—Mr. Beckley, ticket collector on the Cheshire Lines Railway, said he asked the prisoners for their tickets and they said they had none. They said they were going to Sheffield and it was too far to walk. —The Chief Constable said they were both strangers from Sheffield. If they were sent to Man- chester it would help them on a little way. (Laughter). --The prisoners were fined lOs and costs each or fourteen days imprisonment.

Mr. W. D. Houghton's Fortune. Mr: William Dickson Houghton, J.P., of Sankey Wire Mills, Wallington, and Queen's Lodge, Colwyn Bay, proprietor of the Sankey Wire Mills, Sankey Bridges, Warrington,and also of the Don Steel Works, Sheffield, and chairman of the Lancashire Watch Company, Limited, left property which has been valued by his son, Mr. John Houghton, steel wire manufacturer, Mr. Leonard Tatham, of Manchester, solicitor, and Mr. Arthur Appleby Menzies, of the Holt,Prescot,near Liverpool,the executors,at £113,034, with £91,779 net personalty. The will is dated April 22, 1994, by winch testator givos to his wife, Mrs. Katherine Houghton, £l,lOO, such furniture as she may select, the use of the house at Colwyn Bay, or should he have disposed thereof, £l5O a year and the income during her widowhood of £lO,OOO, or £20,000 if she re-marries. Subject to a legacy of £lOO each to his executors, Mr. A. A. Menzies and Mr. L. Tatham, and' the residue is to go his children and the issue of those who may have predeceased him. ASHLEY'S, New Address 4, Buttermarket Street.—Advt Claim by Gartons, Limited. At the Warrington County Court on Thursday, before his Honour Judge Shirees Will, K.C., Messrs. Gartons, Limited, seed specialists, Warrington, sued R. Dorrell, Farmer, Much Wenlock, for £l2 3s. GI for goods supplied.—Mr. Browne appeared for the company and stated that defendant was supplied with some clover seeds in 1903. When pressed for pay- ment of his account he complained that the seeds had been a failure. He had now paid £3 2s. Gd. and propm tionate costs into court. Mr. Harry Pearson, secretary of the coin;:any, stated that seeds identical in quality to thoso supplied to the defendant were tested and of 100 seeds sown 97 were vigorous —a very high percentage.—Defendant alleged that the crop produced was very thin and poor, in fact he contended that the seeds did not produce more than 10 per cent. .His Honour in giving judgment for the plaintiffs for the amount claimed with costs, said that if defendant bad any complaint to make he should have made it at once in writing instead of waiting until be was pressed for the account.

Motor Car Fatality. Thomas Cousens, six years of age was knocked down in Derby-road, Bootle, on Thursday, by a motor car, and sustained injuries from which he died about an hour later at Bootle Hospital. The car was being driven by the owner, William Haddock Robinson, of The Mount, Warrington.— The inquest oa the body was opened on Thursday evening, and, after evidence of identification had been taken, was adjourned until Monday. It appears that the deceased is the son of Robert Cmsens, a timber labourer, who lives at 4, Canal-street,l3ootle.—The Coroner (Mr. S. Brighouse) remarked that,so far as the police could find out up to the present, no blame attached to the driver, who was accompanied by a relative. When the unfortunate occurrence took place he did everything possible for the boy, and saw that he was taken to the hospital. Six ,GUINEAS will purchase a fully guaranteed PREMIER. CYCLE. Inspection invited.—J. S. GAR- AND, 51,53, & 55 Bridge-street, Warrington.:—Advt. Warrington Band of Hope Union. In connection with the festival held at the Parr Hall last week, the whole of the members of the choir and other performers, to the number of between 300 and 400, were entertained to tea at Cairo-street schools, on Thursday evening. The arrangements were in the hands of the Festival Committee and lady workers and were carried out very satisfactorily. After tea an entertainment was given, the items including dialogues, songs and recitations. Mr. T. Dale presided. Mr. F. Gandy (hon. secretary) in the course of a short address congratulated the children upon the magni- ficent results of the ticket-selling and Mr. A. Spruce' (conductor) expressed his satisfaction with their sing- ing. Mr. Hamblett also made a few remarks and a number of prizes were distributed to ticket-sellers who gave in their names too late for the distribution at the festival. A most enjoyable evening was spent and the gathering was a vely fitting conclusion too festival which will rank high in the annals of the Union. ASHLEY'S, New Address 4, Buttermarket Street.—Adv

Board of Guardians. A meeting of the Warrington Thard of Guardians was held at the Workhouse on Wednesday under the presidency of the Rev. T. R. Matthews. There were also present :—Mrs. Wilkinson, Mrs. Simpson, Mrs. Collingwood, Miss Broadbent, Rev. M. Ryan, Dr. Murray, Messrs. G. Mather, J. Billinge, W. Gill W. Hotighton, W. C. Brooka, R. Bolton, P. Longton, A. Brooks, J. C. Sutton (clerk), E. J. Sutton (acting assistant clerk), J. F. Awbery (master), and A. Wright (superintendent of Padgate schaels).—At a meeting of the Padgate Cottage Homes Committee Mr. E. L. Bent was elected chairman and Mr. R. Bolton vice-chair- man. The Rev. G. W. Dickinson was appointed chaplain from May 12th at a salary of £lO per annum, in succession to the Rev. NV. Pollock NHL—The minutes were approved. —At a meeting of the House Committee Mr. J. Billing& was re-elected chairman and Mr. G.Hather vice-chairman. The Medical Officer reported having engaged Dr. Bowden to conduct an examination of probation nurses. The Committee further reported that John Wright having been admitted to the training ship " Indefatigable" the Board be recammended to pay the maintenance charge of £22 per annum and the usual sea outfit. —An invitation from Captain Bremner for the Committee to inspect the ship, and an alterna- tive proposal that he should visit the Cammittee and address them upon its advantages was left to the Board to direct which should take place. It was proposed that the members of the House Committee along with the Master and Superintendent should visit the ship on Thursday next.—Mr. Houghton suggested that a smaller deputation should go. He would not like the Board to get to such a state of degradation that some corporate bodies had reached by such movements.— Mrs. Wilkinson pointed out that the deputation would pay their own expenses, and they shovld.all be entitled to go if they wished.—Mrs. Simpson : I would not go if my expenses were coming out of the institution. The deputation was agreed to as originally pro- posed.—The Chairman extended a hearty welcome to the new lady Guardian, Mrs. Collingwood, and said he hoped they would do all they could- to make her comfortable, and to make all the use they could of her. (Laughter.) —Miss Broadbent, as secretary of the Women Guardians' Association for this district, said she invited Mrs. Collingwood to stand. They were all delighted to welcooe her. —Mr. Billing° also added a few words of congratulation, and at was decided to appoint Mrs. Collingwood a member of the House Committee.—Mrs. Collingwood said she was glad to find herself a member of the Board, and to ba able to take up that new and interesting work. j £l4 14s Good second-hand piano.--Woon,London I rd.; Stockton Heath. I Asillxv's, New Add,ess 4, ifittermarket Street.—Advt Important Case to Colliers. .a.t the Warrington County Court on Thursday, I before his Honour Judge Shiress Will, KG., a case nuder the Workmen's Compensation Act was heard, in which the applicant was Catherine Regan, Burton- wood, and the respondents the Collins Green Colliery I Company.—Mr. Wilson, of Wigan, made the applica- tion on behalf of the Miners' Federation and Mr. I Peace, of Wigan, appeared for the respondents.—Mr. IWilson explained-that applicant's husband was killed j whilst in the employ of the respondents. The firm admitted liability and had paid £2,12 10s. 6d. into court but he (Ur. Wilson) contended that that was not suficient and that Mrs. Regan was entitled to the maximum award (£300). The question to be decided was whether there was a change in the grade of 1 employment which would be equal to a new engage- ment and involve compensation on the higher scale. ; Mr. Wilson contended there had been such a change, as the deceased man was orginally employed as a " metal man " under a contractor but in June 1907 ; he himself became a contractor and the compensation jought to be based on his higher earnings since that date.—Mr. Peace said that the respondents had paid the money into court on the understanding that Regan j was a workman. It had been held that a contractor j could not be a workman within the meaning under j the Act and if Mr. Wilson's point held good the firm were not really liable to pay anything.—Mr. ;Wilson said that when he spoke of a ocaltractor in a colliery he did not mean a contractor in the ordinary sense. It was simply an advance in the man's j industrial position and he continued to receive wages from the Colliery Company.—His Honour found that !Regan was -a contractor and not a workman at the time of his death. That being so the money had been paid into court under a misapprehension and there j was no ground for increasing the amount. —Mr. !Peace said that on that finding the applicant was not entitled to a penny but the firm did not ask to be ! relieved of the voluntary payment they had made.— His Honour directed that the widow should receive £3O ; forthwith and the balance at the rate of 30a. per month. Mr. Peace asked if costs would follow the event. The Miner's Federation was fighting the case.— His Honour said that made no difference to the principle and he ; doubted whether the firm ought to press for costs.— Mr. Peace said that after that expression he would ' not press for them.

ig Dnsustained charge of Damaging Tools. At Daresbury Sessions on uesday Thomas Dawes, of Thelwall-lane, Grappeuhall, was charged with wilfully damaging tools belonging to Perrin's Limited, Grappenhall, to the extent of £l. Mr. F. G. Taylor (Messrs. H.Greenall and Company) prosecuted,and Mr. Browne defended, and pleaded not guilty. Mr. Taylor stated that defendant was employed up to the day before Good Friday by Perrin's, lA., as a socket maker, and the tools for the work required to be very I exact. He understood defendant had some compliant against the works manager, who was too strict, and las he was dissatisfied with his work he gave notice to terminate his employment. On the last two days of his employment he was observed to be using his tools in a most unusual manner, and they con- tended he was wilfully damaging them. What he did was to heat them and in some cases take them to the anvil and cause them to be hit with a sledge hammer. They claimed £1 damage in respect to three of the tools. Hr. Browne said socket making was a peculiar trade and defendant was the only socket maker employed by Perrin's, Limited, He was there for .two years without any complaint. He would tell the Bench that. he heard the firm were going to close down, and that the. management was so incompetent that he decided to get another place. He gave a week's notice to leave and said be mot going to Scotland to get a per- manent place with a good, sound firm. He did nothing whatever to the tools that was not right and consistent, and the tools could be put into perfect condition in hen minutes.—Dawes gave evidence and said the tools produced were good enough for anyone to work with, and he would put them in order in a quarter of an honr.—William Page and Thomas Hill, fitting makers of long experience, examined the tools, and said they were in perfect condition.—Without hearing any farther witnesses the Bench dismissed the case, and allowed the defendant £5 ss. costs. Warrington Musical Festival. Oar readers are reminded that the fiist Warrington Musical Festival will be held at the Parr Hall on Saturday next. From the comeetitive standpoint success is assured and there is also every reason to believe that the public support will be worthy of the occasion. Those who have not already secured tickets should make a point of doing so at the earliest oppor- tunity as a big demand is anticipated. Excellent programmes have been arranged and lovers of music are promised a rich treat. At the afternoon concert, which commences at 2 o'clock, the Mayor (Alderman Smethurst) will preside and the Mayoress will distribute the prizes. The principal items will be the children's action song contest, children's choir contest, and the male voice choral contest. The celebrated Manchester Orpheus Male Voice Choir have entered for the last-named com- petition. The evening concert will begin at 0.30. Mr. A. H. Crosfield, M.P.: will preside and Mrs. A. H. Crosfield has kindly consented to present the winning I choir in the chief choral contest with the valuable l challenge shield which Mr. Crosfield has given. This competition will be the great feature of the festival, 'eight leading mixed choirs of the North having entered. The contest-for church or chapel choirs will be another interesting event as four well-known local choirs will compete. Mr. J. Dodds has presented a challenge trophy which will be handed to the winning choir by Mrs. Dodd% The massed choirs in these competitions nil also sing the test pieces, and a splendid effect wil • doubtless be produced. The artistes who will appear at the festival are Miss Frances Andrews (contralto of Queen's Hall and provincial concerts) and Miss Back- sheen Wood (the 'famous violinist). An interesting biographical sketch of Dr. W. G. MCNaught, the eminent adjudicator, whose services have been secured by the festival committee, appears on page 3.

Sam Ennion, son of Superintendent Ennion,emplo)ed at the County Council offices, Chester, said that on Saturday evening, he was cycling home, when he saw a man in a pit at Rocksavage. He plunged into the water, but the man sank before he could reach him, and he dived and brought. him to the surface and then swam with him to the side. A cyclist and a motorist helped to drag the man, who proved to be the prisoner, up the bank. The prisoner was unconscious, and artificial respiration was applied for forty-five minutest when he recovered. [ Superintendent Ennion spoke to bringing the prisoner to the police station and providing him with dry cloth- ing and rugs. When charged the prisoner said his head had been bad for a few days,. and. he did not know where he went on Saturday. The prisoner said he bad also [ been troubled with influenza, and had been drinking a drop. The prisoner was remanded fora week. Alderman Norman (chairman) said the bench very highly commended the noble way in which Mr. Sam &mien had rescued the man. RURAL DISTRICT COUNCIL. div.head: WHITE CITY.
div.p: THE WHITE CITY.

Bigger and brighter than ever before with a perfect myraid of amusements, culled from all parts of the world, the White City,the creation of J. Calvin Brown, managing director, opens the summer season to-day, wits gala ceremonies. For the past week an army of workmen have been busy, putting the last touches in the " White City for Pleasure" before opening day. To-day will find the high and fast water chute, the new scenic railway, the Initial flight, Iggorrote village, miniature railway, and a host of other amusements in full swing. A thorough test was given the White City's massive electric lighting system on Thursday night shortly after 8 p.m. As the 50,000 or more tiny lights, bidden about the enclosure flashed out in the darkness, hundreds of people gathered in the vicinity of Old Trafford, enrap- tured with the scene, which for artistic effect has never been equalled in England.

div.p: ST. HELEN&
WOMAN'S CURIOUS DEATH.

Caroline Lawton, aged forty-Eli,, of 45, Grant-street, died on Monday in the St. Helens Hospital under some- what curious circumstances. Mrs. Lawton fell in Bridge-street on Thursday,.the 23rd ult., and broke her leg. She was attended by Jr. Knowles, and was making satisfactory progress until Monday, when she collapsed and fell oil her chair. She was lined up and put into bed, and recovered somewhat, but, later rapidly grew worse and died.

A GLASS .WORKS FATALITY. Mr. Brighouse, county corner' held an inquest at St. Helens on Monday on ..N:athan lleuthorne, aged fort} - five, of 22, Marshall's Cross-road, who died In the ht. Helens Hospital from injuries received at the Raven- head plate-glass Works. Mr. Dickinson appeared fur Messrs. Pilkington Brothers, the owners or the works, and Air. liutchen for the relatives.r—itobert Christie, 87, Lyon-street,a producer man, said he was working with Henthorue on Friday morning on a slack platform con- nected with the large gas producers. About a quarter past seven they had finished dis- charging the slack from a waggon, and went to move another waggon to the platform. This had to be barred or levered along for about seven yards. Before moving the waggon be placed a "scotch" on the rail, but the waggon began to move too freely. Witness got another scotch ; for the back wheel, while deceased ran round in front to put the brake down. The waggon went over the first " scotch "and he heard the deceased call out, and found him lying on the ground in front of the waggon, having been crushed between.the.buffers. He was removed to the Stalely:la Hospital, and died the following day.—The jury, who gad inspected the works, returned a verdict of Accidental.death,".and suggested that a block should be•fixed on the rails which would be of such a size that it would prevent the waggon' going any further than was required..

A BEffING APPEAL.
INTERESTING POINT IN A NEWTON CASE.

An interesting point of law under the Betting Act of 1900 was raised before a Divisional Court in the King's : Bench Division, consisting of Justices Darling and Bhillirnore, on Thursday, when Mr. Rigby Swift, on behalf of Matthew Setun, sought an order compelling two of the justices of Newton-in-Maker-field to show cause why their conviction of Seto!) on the 30th of April last should not be brought up and quashed.—The point of error taken was that Soton had been fined £l5 for street betting, it being his first offence under the Act of 1900, though under the Act the penalty for a first. 'offence was limited to £lO. It was true, counsel said, :that Seton had been several times previously convicted for street betting under a local by-law, but his conten- tion was that these should not have been taken into 'account in inflicting punishment for an offence ander the Act of 1003.—Their Lordships granted the rule asked for.

div.head: REFRIGERATING MACHINES .AT THE FRANCO-
div.p: REFRIGERATING MACHINES .AT THE FRANCO-
BRITISH EXHIBITION.

Befrigerating and icemaking machinery seems to become more necessary year by year. This is illus- trated by the fact that Messrs. Lyons and Co. have installed a refrigerating plant at the exhibition for the preservation of the various kinds of pm ishable goods required for the refreshment of the numerous visitors who will be catered for by them. The New South Wales and South Australian Governments have also machines working at their exhibit, an inspection of which is both interesting and instructive. Both these machines are provided by the Linde British Refrigerating Co., Ltd„ who occupy a very prominent. position in the construction of such machinery, having an experience extending over thirty years, and there are now at work all over the world 6,600 machines made by them. Such machinery on the ammonia compression, carbonic acid, and dry air systems has been supplied to the warships of all the principal powers, to numerous mail steamers for the storage of passengers' provisions, and to many cargo steamers for the carriage of frozen , meot. Such machinery also meets with a demand in breweries, cold stores, and of course for icemaking, and there is not only the small electrically driven machine cooling a small box in the butcher's back shop, but there is also the large icemaking machine in a great factory turning out hundreds of tons of ice a day, and the various sizes in between those two limits. Visitors to the Exhibition should not fail to see those machine for even supposing they are not commercially interested, such machinery appeals to the ordinary intelligent mind as an iutetesting illustration of the d..tvelopmeat of science.

div.head: RESCUE AND PREVENTIVE WORK IN LIVERPOOL AND SOUTH-WEST LANCASHIRE.
div.p: RESCUE AND PREVENTIVE WORK IN LIVERPOOL AND SOUTH-WEST LANCASHIRE.

The work of the Police Court Missionaries of th Liverpool Diocesan Branch (Incorporated) of the Church of England Temperance Society has parsued the even tenor of its way, consequently we have nothing startling to report. Nevertheless much good has been done amongst those who have fallen, many being rescued from a life of sin and we ittio.v that such work must be acceptable to our Heavenly Father. During April the missionaries have attended the various courts of the diocese, so as to be ready to take in hand any case that the magistrates—in their discretion—felt might be wisely placed in their care. In the courts and In idewell the missionaries sought conversations with the prisoners and found success in 1,203 cases. This resulted—amongst other unseen results —in 89 pledges being taken—in work being found at our Firewood Factory for 26 additional men in employment being obtained in other channels for 17 boys and men— in 11 boys being restored to their friends, It•ho other- wise might still be roaming the streets getting into mischief, and in 41 women and girls being restored to their friends or placed in homes. During the month the Mission Room at Walton Gaol has been opened each morning, except on Sunday, at 7 a.m and 670 discharged prisoners availed themselves ef the hospitality of the missionaries and partook of Neakfast. Upon 39 occasions the men and women were addressed and exhorted to amend their ways. It: is necessary to make a great effort in order to do this, but when this is made, it is by the grace of God, often successful. Three hundred and fifty-six discharged prisoners visited the missionaries either at their homes or office. Efforts were made to give these people anew start—by letters to various employers and friends—of which 312 were penned. In 39 cases clothing was supplied so that situations might be filled, which other- wise, could not have been accepted. Destitute cases numbering 38 were supplied with food. At the request of the magistrates and police 198 cases were given special attention. Rescue work, which is sometimes so depressing, is not the only work of the Society. We have a muck brighter side, that which is called " Preventive," carried on so ably under the direction of Mr. E. Craw- shaw (day school lecturer), and Mr. H. Ilankey (Band of Hope organizer.) The examinations, by means of which we find out some of the results of their winter's work amongst the children, were held during April, and the result of the examiner's report is that St. Philip's Band of Hope, Liverpool, find themselves at the top, and have therefore won the banner. Eight papers by Liverpool children have been sent to London to com- pete for the National Challenge Banner. This is very useful work, and we look to it to form a better and healthier national opinion in the future which will make itself evident in a more sober people. Donations to the work may be sent to the Key. P. W. Pheysey, 11, Lord-street, Liverpool.

div.head: POLITICS OF THE WEEK.
div.p: THE POLITICS OF THE WEEK.
[F1:01,1 OUR LONDON COIRINrOYDAST.]

We are nearly at the end of the by-elections, so that next week, after something like a miniature General Election reflecting political excitement in all parts of the country except Ireland, which has hem free from election excitement,attention will be again concentrated on Parliament, and a lively time there it will be for the measures now developing at Westminster touch the life of the country at many points. Our schools, our houses, the planning of our towns,enr clubs, our food, and cur freedom to import it cheaply, our drink, our poor children, our poor old men and women and their new pensions, our workers underground, our great port of London and our smallest rural bamlets,besides the peasantry of the whole of Scotland, and those who , are thirsting for the higher education in Ireland—all these topics of vital interest and importance in the daily life of the nation, and others easy to overlook on a general survey, our present Government are concerning themselves within this very Session. Who, after this, can say that politics are not of real interest? Who can keep up the ridiculous affectation of indifference to what is going on in the political world, and boast that he never gives a vote ? llt is a confession, happily, rarely made, for it means Ithat those who make it ate silly enough not to take any interest in what are really their own affairs.

div.head: MR. CHURCHILL'S RETURN.
div.p: MR. CHURCHILL'S RETURN.

On Monday, the new President of the Board of Trade, Mr. Churchill, came back to the House of Commons, fresh from Dundee. There was not much indifferenre to politics in that election, and facts and arguments had a fair run. Jute is the steple trade of Dundee, znd jute is bard hit by competition from ' abroad ; but it is competition mainly of iranufactorers in our own great Indian Empire where the raw inatelial is grown, and where it has long been fors( m that jute manufacture must in the natural course of things grow and thtive. It would be interesting to know how far Dundee's capital and Dundee's sons a-e profiting from the native prosperity. In any case, tariff reform remedies did not appeal to the people of Dundee, even during the depression of jute manu- facture. Nor was the election seriously affected by the influence of the licensed trade. The licensing Bill does rot apply to Scotland, and Scottish senti- ment is far ahead of English opinion on ,the question of public control of the liquor traffic. The big danger to Mr. Churchill was the activity of the Labour party, which, though already represented by Dundee's other member, Mr. Wilkie, aspired to the possession of both Feats ; and with such encouragement that the Labour candidate's own agent predicted his success and Lad visicals of a poll of over 7000. But it was 'Mr. Churchill who had the 7000, and Mr. Stuart had to be content with 4000 in which vote he. nearly equalled the [niorist candidate. Although there was a fourth candidate, Mr. Churchill's victory was decisive. It was so recognised in the warmth of the greeting which he had in the House of Commons. The Prime Minister paid Dundee, as well as his colleagues, a compliment by escoi ting him to the table.

div.head: IT RCOLTRT FOR MONTROSE.
div.p: A IT RCOLTRT FOR MONTROSE.

Montrose followed the example of Dvidee, and sent up a day or two later to the House of Commons, as its member, a son of the late Sir William Harcourt, who arrives appropriately, when a great Budget is unfolded which is only possible becsuse of his father's memor- able stroke in national finance—the Death Duty Budget. It must be pleasing to every House of Commons man, irrespective of Tarty, to see in St. Stephen's the two sons of the great Liberal, who, next to the late Sir }ferny Campbell Bannerman himself, was the staunchest champion of his party even in the days of its adversity. The new membei's brother, Jr. Lewis Hareoutt, is one of the brightest members of Mr. Asquith's brilliant Cabinet,a universal favourite, absolutely without pretentioucleos and self-assettion, and commanding in s he of his modesty ageneral and even enthusiastic recognition of his merit. So Mr. Robe' t Hat court, apart from his own services to his party in his contests at Hastings and Montrose, is sloe of a double welcome as his father's son, and as the brother of the amiable and brillisnt First Commissioner of Works. HOUSING.

The lobust and energetic Mr. Long publicly com- plained that the great Bill of this week—Mr. Burns's Housing Bill had given him a headache. The allusion was to the difficulty of understanding what is called "legislation by reference." Now-a-days a great many Parliamentary Bills are amendments and extensions of half-hearted refonns of earlier times, and it is hard to understand the new measures unless you have the old Acts before you. Both of the great patties in the State have promised to do their best to get rid of this kind of law, and to give us in each statute something that can be understood of ittelf. But before that can be done it is necessary to have some guarantee that it will not re -open the floodgates of discussion on points alveady embodied in law. The alternative is often either no legisln tints at all, or legislation by reference. Mv. Burns's Bill, however, is not so "headachy " as Mr. Long suggests, and it is meant to cure a great deal_ of heartache over the comparative failure of previous Housing Bills. Me ty cf the scandals of housing could he swept a way under the existing law if the authorities cared to adopt portions of it which ale what is called " permissive. ' Fcr many reasons (including the good reason of fear to increase rates and lose public money in arbitrations, lawyeis' fees. extravagant comi -nsation and EO on) the powers of the law have not Leen used, and one of the reasons for new legislation is to take away these excuses for inaction and to give the unenterprising autholity a push. Mr. Burns has set before him a bright ideal home healthy, house beautiful, town pleasant, city dignified, and subutb salubrious." He wants to " abolish the slums,"" efface ghettoes of meanness and Alsatias of squalor." The housing problem is as acute in the rural districts, perhaps acuter, certainly less easily solved, than in the town (for economic and social reasons), and this is the big problem that Mr. John Burns has tackled. TOWN PLANNING.

The novel part of Mr. Burns's scheme is its provi- sions for " town planning"— a phrase better known on the Continent than at home. It mears laying out in advance the lines on which a town is to develop, care being taken for the interspacing of dwellings with breathing and recreation places, trees, gardens, minia- ture parks, and an effort being made to avoid dulness and uniformity in the laying out of streets and so forth. The importance of these schemes for own dwellers is now well established scientifically. What sotncls idealistic is really severely practical. Disease and death are found to be closely related to density of population. Too many houses together, too few lungs "for your city or your town mean an unenvi- able place in the Pegistrar's vital statistics. WILL BARMAIDS BE ABOLISHED?

In the big struggle on the Licensing Bill, appeals to sentiment play a big F.rt. There has been much heart melting reference to the widows and orphans who are said to be interested to an alarming extent ;-1 brewery investments ; and a not less effective appeal to the sentimental side of the public has been made on behalf of the barmaids. The advertisement calling the meeting of 'barmaids ar.d women assistants at Holborn Town Hall this wcek wash. ,ded " Abolition of Barmaids." Two 3.l.P.'is—one of them the high- toned Lord Robert Cecil—bad their names advertised under these suggestive words—survestive, certainly, not of truth. Bow many people, who have not time to read Parliamentary bills,or long Parliamentaty debates ate believing at this moment that the Licensing Bill is really going to abolish barmaids ? In sober fact, all that the Bill dces is to give licensing justices the power, where they see fit to make it one condition among others of the renewal of a licence that women shall not serve in the bars. It no more follows that they will make this condition than that they will refuse music or dancing licences. All will depend on the circumstances of each particular case.

div.head: HOPS AGAIN.
div.p: HOPS AGAIN.

The House of Lords had a d;scussion this week on the hop industry, the result being that Lord Carring- ton had an opportunity of bringing cut the main facts that are being established 12. fore Sir William Collins's Committee, and demonstrating in advance the difficulty of meeting any trouble of this kind by foreign import duties. To begin with it was shown that a 40s. duty 1 on hops, which is what is asked, will not be sufficient to keep the Californian bops out. The duty would have to be increased. These tbings always go on from bad to worse. Then the brewers cannot do with- out a proportion of foreign hops. Beer-drinkers have been educated up to a beer flavoured partly with foreign bops, and they will not like the beer without , them. Again, the Kentish farmer, or the Worcester , one, who does not grow hops, will demand something to protect him from foreign competition. And the brewer, and his shareholders, will say, " You are ruining our profits ; you must compensate us by taking something off our excise duty." div.head: WIDOW BURNT TO A CINDER.
div.p: WIDOW BURNT TO A CINDER.
Shocking Fatality at Warrington.

Coroner S. Brighouse conducted an inquest at the Police Station on Monday morning concerning the terrible death of a woman named Elizabeth Binns Brookes, 69, who resided with her son Albert Edward Brookes' at 29, Lloyd-street. Percy Brooltes, 31, Liverpool-road, said his mother (the deceased) suffered from dropsy, and it was her custom to sleep near the kitchen fire, which she kept butaing all night. His brother, Albert Edward was an epileptic and was of weak intellect. Ho last saw her alive abont five weeks ago. He was told she was in the Warrington Market last Wednesday, but he did not see her. . _

Albert Ethvard Brookes said he wan ft Cosporatioi! scavenger, and was subject to fits. 'lce deceased urts ' his mother. He rent to bed at eleven o'clock on Satur- day night, leaving his mother clearing the supper things I away. At 3.15 the following morning he awoke and found the room full of smoke. He opened the window and roused a neighbour named Welsby. Thomas Welsby said he was a soap works labourer, , and rrsided at 27, Lloyd-street. Tue last witness , informed him that his house was on fire. He tried to enter the house, but was compelled to retire owing to the smoke and flames. He then ran to the fire station and informed P.C. Andrews. He never saw the deceased but she was very secluded and retired. P.C. Andre"-s said at 3.30 a.m. he met Wels'oy in I Priestley-street. From what he said witness hurried to I Brooke's house. Albert Edward Brookes,who was standing' outside, called out, " Our horse is on fire." Witness • asked him if there was anyone inside, and he said, "Yes, my mother is upstairs in the hack room." It was a four ; roomed house. Witness searched both bedrooms, which . were full of smoke, but failed to find anybody. After • opening the windows be Came downstairs and found a fire raging furiously in the front kitchen. The heat and , smoke prevented witness entering. With a few buckets of water he put out the thmes. The house W 4,9 in dark- I ness and he turned on his lamp to make a search when ; the Fire Brigade arrived. In the corner, where the fire had been, witness found the body orthe deceased, which had Leen terribly burnt. She was lying on her back and underneath her were the charred remains of a wooden chair. The pictures on the walls had been blistered with the heat, and the box of a sewing machine • was also partly damaged. Some clothes on the back of the door and the door had been ecorched, as though Mrs. ; Brookes whilst on tire, had tried to get out. On the hearth witness saw a piece of half-burnt coal, which ' apparently bad fallen off the fire. The door leading to the street was locked and the key inside. Witness con- veyed the body to the mortuary. Dr. Smith said he examined the body. The legs were only burnt superficially, but the upper part of the body was burnt practically to a cinder. There were I only the charred remains of the skull, the left arm was burnt clean away, while the right arm was reduced to; a cinder. Ile was of opinion that Mts. Brooks' skirt caught fire, that she went to the bottom of the stairs to call her son, that she then went back and collapsed on the chair and was burnt to death. She must have been; burning two or three hours. She was very fat, and that no doubt accounted for the extensive burning of the body. The chair was burnt to charcoal, but the rest of the fuiniture was practically intact Alice Leigh, a girl about eleven years old. gave evidence to seeing the deceased at ten o'clock on I Saturday night when she bade her " Good-night." IThe ;Jury after a moment's consideration returned _a , verdict of Accidental death." - - -
„. The Coroner then asked the constable to step in the box. - - _

The Coroner: How long have you been in the Force. The Constable : Six years. The Coroner: I don't know what the jai g think, but I think you displayed a great amount of what is a very scirce commodity at the present time—that is common- sense. I think you did e,rerything that could possibly be done and showed that you had your brains about you in searching the house in the way you did. I think you ought to be highly commended. The jury also congratulated the officer on his conduct,

313/ DEAR CHILDREN, 0 I am very pleased indeed that my mem- bers are increasing, and that a large number of these are sending me nice letters. I am sure that my nieces and nephews will quite under- stand that it is impossible for me to publish all their communications, but I am always most pleased to hear from them. As far as possible I try to print the stories, etc., received. I must thank Fred Nuttall 'and Annie Barnes for a long list of new members. To both these mem- bers I am sending a little present in return for their trouble in trying to make our Corner more known. Every member joining is re- quired to promise something. It is very simple, and it is to be kind to all dumb animals. I want our League to be "doing something," and I am sure that if every member will try and be kind and also try to stop cruelty to animals he of she will be doing a good work. What do my members think? I must thank Bessie Lewis for a nice letter (printed further down these columns). This member has also sent me her photo. Ido hope more zuember v will follow hoz example, _ . _ _ _
Don't forget ±h-se prize books offered for the best account of "Hdw I spent Easter," to be sent in during the coming week. With love, UNCLE IN ED.

What a beitutiful day for the Ist of May; quite a change. It is so nice in Spring to go for a walk and see all the flowers and hear the birds singing, especially a day like this. I suppose we shall soon hear the cuckoo calling. On Easter Thursday we had a missionary enter- tainment and bazaar. We were all dressed as Chinese boys and 'girls, and we took 6E13, which was very good considering it was such a small bazaar. Our branch of the Young People's Union supports a missionary in Africa. It is very amusing to hear the funny things they do in China. The ladies wear trousers and men petticoats. They shake their own hands. Boys turn their back to the schoolmaster when say- ing their lessons. On the other hand it is very sad to hear the dreadful things they do. Opium smoking is like a curse to China. The smoker will not only pawn his wife and children's clothing, but will often sell the stones of his house, and then sell his wife and children. He would get about 30s. for a little girl aged 11. I hope yOu will not be too bored with read- ing this letter. I expect you know all this Already. BESSIS LEWIS.
THE BLIND BLIND GIRL Ahi many a one remembers The blind and gentle child; None. other. was so good and wise,
So beautiful and She walk'd into the village To school in days bygone, And all: the way from step to step

.. - The children 'led her on. And every one cared for her; They loved to be her stay, And sought to guide her steps along Thro' all the weary way. The children spoke of meadows, And paths athwart the lea, And of the roses 'neath her feet, But blind, ah blind was she. She heard the heaven-born music
Of birds among the -trees, And felt upon her little face The sunbeam and the breeze; The roses cast their fragrance/

To cheer her heart aw-hile, But she saw not the sunshine fair, Nor e'en her mother's smile. The child lies yonder buried— When at death's, door she lay She at her mother smiled and said, "I see the dawn of day." She soar'd in light and glory From parti and tumult wild; And gazing on the scenes of heav'n Lives now the poor blind child! G. E. WARD.
-÷-- DO HORSES KNOW SUNDAY?

The carriage horses of a friend of mine were accustomed on weekdays to take out their mis- tress for an early drive before lunch, while on Sundays they did not do so. On weekdays they were never known to lie down in the mornings before the time they usually went out vMh their mistress, but on Sundays they never missed doing so. It seemed as though the noble and wise animals were determined to make the most of •their day's rest._
'MONA SCOTT.

div.head: DREAMS.
div.p: DREAMS.

We lived qut under the pear tree, We dined upon tarts and cream, I married you there for ever, But, dear, twas only a dream! We tailed away in the branches To countries strange and new, For we owned estates in Dreamland, But, sweetheart, it isn't true! We made a church in the pear tree Where the angels came to sing, We stroked their wings, but, dearest, You musn't believe a thing( We cut our names in the tree trunk, So the bark could never grow; And the Dryad cried: "But, my darling, 'Twas none of it really so I" ' FLORENCE RESTALL. THE YOUNG DOCTOR.

Gerald liked playing at being a doctor. He put his father's hat on and took his thick stick, and went to see how Ella's big doll was. When he was older he learned to be a doctor. Sometimes he had to pound drugs in a mortar and sometimes he attended medical lectures. When he was older he became the doctor to a children's hospital.. When the war broke out he went to the Crimea as an army surgeon. Oftimes in great danger he attended to the wounded men, and was so brave that when he returned to England the Queen presented him with a medal, and condescended to pin it on his coat. By this time Ella was quite grown up. Gerald heard she was very ill. He visited her many times and was glad she had not forgotten him. When she was quite well again they were married. The children strewed flowers before them, and they had a beautiful wedding cake. NORA L. MOORING.

div.head: BIRD AND THE SUN.
div.p: THE BIRD AND THE SUN.

"Mother," said a'young bird, looking out of his hole in the wall on a cold wintry day, "What has become of the flowers?" "They lie deep down under the snow, my son." "And what has become of all the nice fruits, mother? Where are they now?" "They are gone, my son." "And the gay flies, mother, with the bright wings, where are they?" "Dead, al dead, my son." "And the creeping things, mother, that we live on, where are they?" " Safe under the earth, my son." "Oh, mother, how dreary it is then! We have nothing at all left." "Well," said The old bird, "it is dreary now; but look up at the sun that shines in the heavens. He still re- mains to us, and will soon bring back the flowers and the fruit and all our needful food. Then let us wait and trust, my son, for in time we shall have all things, though they are now hidden from our sight." FLOSsrE NEALE.

If I knew the box where the smiles were kept, No matter how large the key, Nor how strong the bolt, I would try so hard, 'Twould open I know for me. Then over the land and the seaboard coast I'd scatter the smiles to play, That the children's faces might hold them fast For many and many a day. If I knew the box that was large enough

To hold all the frowns I meet, I would like to gather them every one From nursery, school, and street. I'd pack them in and turn the monster key; I'd hire-.a giant to drop the box To the depths of the deep, deep sea. ETHEL S. OWEN.
EACH THOUGHT THE OTHER STUPID.

A tall stranger walked into the post office the other day and inquired whether there were any letters for him. The postmaster asked, "What name, please?" "Louder," replied the man, and the postmaster raised his voice and asked again, ",The name, please." "Louder," again replied the stranger. Upon this the postmaster sang out in angry tone, "Your name, please." The angry inquirer then shouted, "Louder, James Louder. Can't you hear ? " NEVILLE V. SCOTT. MAKING TEA.

"Mamma has got a headache," Said thoughtful little May; "I think I'll make a cup of tea, I'm sure I know the way. The kettle boils, the pot is warm, Next I must fetch the tea; Two spoonsful surely is enough -Just for mamma and me. Arid now I'll make a piece of tdast, Just crisp and brown you know; And now the cloth is on the tray, A cloth as white as snow." Then entering soft at mother's door These words fall on her ear, "Some tea for me, I am so glad. Oh, thank you, May, my dear." FAitNY RAYIsOULD. THE NEW MAID.

Master: "Oh, will you get me my boots?" Maid: "If what?' Master: "Oh, if you please." Maid: "If you please what?" Master: "Will you kindly get me 'my boots, if you please, miss?" Maid: "That's better. No, I won't!" • The story is told of the late Professor Blackie that when he once put a card on the door of his lecture-room, reading: "Professor Blackie will meet his classes at one p.m.," some waggish student obliterated the " c " in " classes.".llap- pening to pass that way the old professor saw the change. Stepping up to the door he obliterated the letter "1," and went grimly on his way without a; word.

GORTON MURDERER EXECUTED.

The execution took place at Strangeways Prison on' Tuesday morning of John flarnshottom, of Gorton, who shot his brother-in-law. He passed a good night, ate a hearty breakfast, and walked firmly to the scaffold. Pierpeint was the executioner. A crowd of several hundreds of people, mostly females, assembled in the vicinity of the prison about the hour fixed for the execution.—At the inquest the medical evidence was to the effect that death had been instantaneous.
