div.head: VALUE OF A GOOD BICYCLE.
div.p: THE VALUE OF A GOOD BICYCLE.

To those who know the difference between cycles it is always a matter for regret that those who can least afford the money should so often be misled by cheap. Jack advertisements when there are so many firat-class bicycles in the market at reasonable prices. If only those whose knowledge of cycling is confined to the bicycle of unknown name could have en experience of a first-class machine, a Humber for instance, they would realize what they have missed. A typ:. .1 instance is afforded in a letter from Mr. F. 11. Leng, of Great Limber, near Brocklesby, Lincs., who writes that he has ridden his Humber about 35 miles daily and "it has been well tested " especially as his weight is 15 stone. " The cycles that I have had " continues Mr. Leng, "have always been cheap machines, and have soon been out of order, but the Humber looks as if it is going to bi e the best n the long run." Yet a Humber can be bought as low as seven guineas—for adult's machines— and moreover the ifunil.3r Company has by for the most equitable system of easy payment of any firm. Before baying a bicycle, no ratter how specious the advertisements, intending cyclists would be well advised to consult the local Humber agents or depots, and get the Humber terms. No cyclist will ever go wrong in buying a Humber, and the prices are so low and the easy payments so equitable and reasonable, that there is no reason why anyone should be debarred.

Mr. King, M.P. and Unemployment. Speaking at Alsager on Saturday,Mr. A. J. King, M.P. for Knutsford, said that a great deal had been said about the number of persons who would be thrown out of employment if the Licensing Bill were passed. But there was not a trade in the country that paid less for labour in proportion to its turnover than the brewing interest. For every pound spent in tho getting of coal lls, went in wages; in the cotton trade ss. 4d. ; and on the railways Es. 3d. But in the drink trade for every pound turned over the amount paid in wages was is. Ed. It was said that the" trade " contributed 38 millions a year to the revenue of thebountry, but that money had first of all to be collected from the people. (Hear, hear, and laughter). While he recognised the value of a solid Labour party in the House of Commons, he expressed the hope that the Labour party in the country would not divide the progressive forces and help to hand seats to others who were not in sympathy with the Labour interest. The Brewer's Attitude. "BY TENS CRAFT WE HAVE OUR WEALTH." The great outburst of anger and indignation on the part of the members of the liquor traffic at the intro- duction of the new Licensing Bill brings to mind another cry, mentioned in the Acts of the Apostles,that of the Ephesian Demetrius, concerning his trade of shrine-making for the worship of the false god Diana. When the Apostle Paul in his preaching denounced the people for their false worship, Demetrius found his traffic of idols was likely to suffer. He called together the workmen in the trade, and said unto them, " Sirs, ye know by this Draft we have our wealth." And when I they heard these sayings they were full of wrath, and cried out, saying, " Great is Diana of the Ephesians." I Acd now our ears are assailed by another such cry, that of the brewers, the publicans, and the shareholders; another great trade by which much money is made and great wealth produced to the detriment and destruction of thousands of men and women and little children ; thousands of pounds in profits and dividends wrung from the drink-stricken victims engaged in the worship of the alcoholic god Bacchus. The trade could hardly be less sound financially than it is to-day, not as a result of the legislation, but of the nonsensical, stupendous, and monstrous over-capitalisa- tion which took place over ten years ago, when all the brewers rushed and floated their companies and businesses into limited liability concerns ; and when the public rose like 'fish to the bait of the brewers, they swallowed all that was offered in the way of large promises in good faith. The money of the widows and the orphan chil- dren which they prate about was taken and used for the widening out of this trade, whieh for so many years has fattened and flourished on the blood and tears of the manhood, the womanhood, and the childhood of the nation. The work of the brewers is to brew, and not to go about buying up and purchasing at exorbitant prices the public-houses in the land, and binding and tying the publicans to sell their particular beer and no other, whether it be good, bad, or indifferent, and whether the public want it or not. "Good Words." A Great Temperance Measure Bishop of London's Strong Support. The Bishop of London presided over a great meeting of the London Diocesan Branch of the Church of England TeMperance Society,held at the Queens's Hall, London, on Monday night. He sturdily maintained his snpp ,rt cf the Licensing BRIJ-Ind kept the meeting enthusiastic, no sign of dissent being manifested during his speech. A special prayer asked for Divine help in " all our fighting against the deadly sin of intemperance, espicially in this great diocese!' The Bishop of London made one of his characteristic- ally direct colloquial and downright speeches. I am always very proud, he said, when I lead my temperance army. ..I do not think there is a more enthusiastic and

their opposition upen the effect (or supposed effect. , which is a very different thing) on their finance and I:property interests. Little or no consideration has been ' given to the well-being of the people, or to intemperance as the great impediment to national , progress. I In regard to the right to a vested interest in the I monopoly value the trade.have no case and they know it, only those who know nothing of the legal history or national custom are rash enough to put forward the !•clalm. I venture to think that I can establish this ,point beyond doubt with anyone who cares to discuss it. I have no wish to lengthen this correspondence, all the more so as the point between Mr. Rylands and I myself was not that of the monopoly value, but the 1 goodwill which Mr. Rylands considered as separate from this value, and entitled to compensation if the I monopoly value were taken away by tee non-renewal .of the licence at the end of the time limit. It does not seem to me the goodwill in the case of tied houses (over ninety per. cent, of the whole) is worth much or need be lost, and Ido not see there is a valid claim upon the State for. consideration. Let me illustrate the point. Suppose I have certain premises which I let on an annual tenancy, the arrangement is renewed for many years. In course of time I require the premises, or to make the case more akin, I find that the character of the business does not add to the respectability of my surrounding property, and I tell my tenant that he must give up the premises at the en 4 of the year. He pleads that he had built up a business, established a goodwill on the expectancy of renewal. I admit that it may be a little bard upon him and in a generous moment decide to give him a fourteen years' notice. I do this presumably because of this goodwill which might he lost. This being so why should I have to consider the goodwill again at the end of the fourteen years ? The cases are not parallel in every point but they are so in essentials and as far as Mr. Rylands' point is concerned viz. the right to compensation for goodwill after a fourteen years' notice. Mr. Rylands talks of my being driven to cover and referring the point to amendment in Committee. Ido not think there is anything in the point, at the same time it is a legitimate one to be raised in Committee. It does not affect the principle of the Bill which is a 1 resumption of the full and free power to deal with the monopoly value which power was restricted by the Act of 1891. To imply as Mr. Rylands does that the recovery of , this power by means of the time limit has uo relation 1 to temperance appears to me contrary to reason. To describe my remarks about drunkenness as a "diatribe" and as obscuring the issue by a cloud of words is neither fair nor justifiable. I said nothing about drunkenness, or the tied house system which was not accurate, moderate, and to the point. The question of the regu- lation and issue of licences is only of importance in relation to intemperance. I have no interest in it apart from this, and whether the trade like it or not this relation will have to be acknowledged and discussed. I will now deal with Mr. Rylands' three points, First. Dislocation of employment. Mr. Rylands' estimate of three persons in the licensed houses likely to be closed is ample becsuse it will be the small, redundant, and unprofitable houses that will he closed. This gives for the 30,000 houses to be closed during fourteen years 90,000 persons. There are 9,000 deaths per year in the retail trade (more propor- tionately than in any other trade, even the most dangerous). Over fourteen years this will give 120,000. Take off 16,000 for the proportion due to the reduction of total number and you have 110,030 deaths against a displacement of 90,000. These and more will be required to fill the gaps caused by death in the houses continued. What then becomes of Mr. Rylands' "serious dislocation in employment ?" Second. The effect on weak Brewing Companies which may be embarassed by the passing of the Bill. When We recall the fact that since the introduction of the Bill every possible method has been used to create alarm and depress stocks, in spite of this the investing public have net taken these gloomy forebodings seriously and the drop in brewing shares has been comparatively small, and not more than the drop in -nr •

united body of fighters for Christ in the world, and I am particularly glad to meet them to-night, because I particularly want to be backed up by my own army in this fight. Remember that we polled eleven bishops out of sixteen—and that is some- thing. (Cheers.) lam going to speak first of all of the great enemy we have to Sight. As Igo on and take up new branches of church work I become more and more keen about temperance endeavours. In one year 145,000 children died in England under the age of twelve months, and Mr. Sims (whose figures I can trust) says that 47:0,000 children per annum are cruelly neglected. That means half a million children driven to an early death and to life-long misery. Why ? Not became parents are naturally unkind to their children. They are more inclined to spoil them than be unkind to them. In nine cases out of ten this awful holocaust of children is caused by drink. AT GRIPS WITH A GRE tT ENEMY'. The other day (the Bishop of London continued) for a change I thought of a midnight march. I am a respectable, steady-going man, accustomed to go to bed in good time—when I can get through my letters. But for a change I thought I would go out to the good old Church Army. We took out a grand band and a line lot of torches, and we sucked dry 13 or 11 public. houses. If at half-past one in the morning you had looked at our congregation—drunken or half- drunken men, comparatively—you would have real- ised the results of the drink tragic in England. How do we fight against this evil ? First by encourag- ing useful legislation. lam one of those who believe that 90,000 public-houses in England is a great deal too many—(cheers)---and therefore. although I do not consider the Licensing Bill an ideal measure, I am delighted to support it, for when it becomes law it will reduce those licences by 30,000, which is an admirable thing.—(Cheers.) A BREWER'S TESTIMONY. The other day I was speaking to a friend of mine—a brewer—and it is one of my regrets that I have to take action against my personal friends, for I must always acknowledge the tray in which the brewers backed up I the work of the church in the East End of London. He told me that whenever a public-house is closed in the East End the custom is not transferred to neighbouring ' houses ; it evaporates. Then I say, this is a great ! temperance bill. (Cheers.) I 'am in favour of some- thing like a favoured-nation treatment for the public- houses which survive the time limit. (Cheers). The Bishop went on to say : "We propose to face this tremendous problem, first by encouraging useful legislation, secondly by reclaiming the drunkard, and thirdly by saving the children." Town Council Supports Licensing Biii. Nelson Town Council on Wednesday night unani- mously adopted a resolution supporting the Licensing Bill, and honing that the Government would further strengthen the law relating to the regulation and super- vision of clubs.

Jp in similar securities outside the area affected by this Bill. All the widows and orphans can to-day get out at a small loss, that is as far as the effect of this Bill is concerned. Of course the depreciation which has been going on for some years is permanently lost. Thin% The possibility of the increase of the con- sumption of spirits through the closing of house where beer is principally consumed. Mr. Rylands emphasizes this danger by referring to the increase in number of beer houses in the early part of last centuary the result of the Beer Act of 1830. Mr. Rylands rightly states that this was enacted to counteract spirit drinking, but he is entirely wrong when he goes on to state that it accom- plished its purpose, i.e. if the purpose was to make a more sober people. A Licensing Commission in their report used these words in reference to this Act, "Never was an Act passed which so disastrously failed to fulfil the expectation of its Authors." Not only did the con- sumption of beer increase, but spirits as well. A Com- mission of the House of Lords reported in 1850 "It appears that the multiplication of houses for the con- sumption of intoxicating liquors (which under the Beer Act has risen from 88,930 to 123,396)has been an evil of the first magnitude. Coincident with this increase in the facilities for intoxication, it appears crime has increased in a frightful ratio (the increase was over fifty per cent)." This increase of drunkenness and crime noted in 130 went on no less rapidly until the fetal policy of unrestricted facilities for beer drinking, which :qr. Itylanda commends, was reversed by tho Licensing Acts of 1830 to 1871 Soon after this reversal the increase of drunkenness and its attendant crime began to decrease. Lecky in his History of England tells us that at the beginning of the Eighteenth Century Parliament released its hold on the drink trade and the previous regulations were repealed. An orgy of drunkenness followed. The famous signs 1" Drunk for a penny, dead drank for twopence, clean straw for nothing" appeared on numerous drinkshops ; a vast part of the population sank straightway to the lowest depth of degradation and it was only the influence of wise laws and an opposite policy that slowly effected a partial rescue. lan disposed to accept Mr. Lecky's record before the opinion of Mr. Rylands' especially when it is backed by the authority of many other writers. I thank Mr. Rylands for turning my attention to this period in the history of the Licensing Trade because it speaks strongly for the Bill. If in the past through the increase of facilities,consumption, drunkenness, and crime, all increased, is it not reasonable to expect that a reduction in unnecessary facilities (which is what this Bill will accomplish) will be accompmied by a decrease in consumption, drunkenness, and crime? The Trade do net desire the two last, but they fight the Bill because they at least know, if Mr. Rylends is still in doubt, that the consumption will be affected where it approaches and reaches the point of excess. Drunken- ness is in no small measure the product of its oppor- tunities. The more public-houses there are, the more temptations there are to the weak, the keener become the efforts of the competitors for custom and the less scrupulous are found to be the methods they use. Remove the excessive opportunities and you reduce the ' drunkenness they produce. CHARLES E. PARKER. ' Penketh, May 13th 1933.

Local Free Churches and the Bill. At a meeting of the Free Church Council of Warring- ton and District held on Wednesday evening, at which the representatives of the wrious Freo Churches of Warrington and district were present, a resolution was unanimously carried that a petition in favour of the Bill be sent to the Prime Minister and the local Member.

PENICETIf LIBERAL CM:B.—The Liberal Club held their annual fleeting on Thursday evening. The mem- bers, who numbered 38, sat clown to tea as the guests of the President, the tea having been prepared by Mr. J. Routledge. After tea the business meeting was held, and the President (Mr. R. Routledge) occupied the chair. Mr. H. Cheetham, the treasurer,read the balance sheet which was well received by the members as a very satisfactory statement. The election of officers was then proceeded with. The President was re-elected for the ensuing year, also the secretary, Mr. Herbert Davies and Mr. Harold Cheetham, treasurer. The mem- bership of the club bas increased during the year the number being about O.

div.head: Examiner, Saturday, May 16, 1903.
div.p: The Examiner, Saturday, May 16, 1903.
" OBSERVER " COMPANY'S!
4FFAIRS. _- BIG REDUCTION OF CAPITAL. -- Never Paid a Dividend. BUSINESS TRANSFERRED TO MESSRS. MACKIE & CO., LTD.

At the Watrington County Court, on Thursday, before his Honour Judge Shiress Will, K.C., Mr. F. M. Preston, barrister (instructed by Messrs. Woods and son, Warrington), applied on behalf of the " Observer " Printing and Publishing Co., Ltd., for sanction to a reduction of capital of the Company. He stated that the registered office of the company was in Warrington, and the issue of capital was under 1...10,000, so that that was the proper .Court before which to bring the petition for a reduction of capital—Mr. Preston pfoceeded to read the petition which set forth the fact that the campany was incorporated in 1393, with regis- tered offices at Bewsey Chambers to carry on the business of newspaper proprietors and printers. The capital was :C5,000 divided into 10,000 shares of 103. each. The company had issued 6,520 of those shares and 10s. per share had been paid up thereon. The articles of association gave power to the company to resjuce its capital from time to time by special resolu- tion. Such a resolution had been passed, reducing the capital from £5,000 divided into 10,000 shares of 10s. each to £1,500 divided into 10,009 shares at 33. each, such reduction to be effected by cancelling capital which has been lost or is unrepresented by available assets to the extent of 7s. per share on each of the 6520 shares now outstanding and reducing the nominal amount of all shares in the company's capital from 103. to 3s. per share. That meant that the capital was henceforth to be .£1,500 divided into 10,000 shares of 3s. each instead of the original capital of i.-'5,000 divided into 10,000 shares of 103. each. At the time of the registration of the minutes 6,520 of the said shares had bean issued on each of which 33. had been paid and the remaining 3,430 were unissued. Mr. Preston asked his Honour that the addition to the name of the company of the words " arid reduced " should be discontinued.

The Judge said he must have some reason given. Mr. Preston produced the affidavit of Thomas E. Withington,Calcheth Hall, chairman of the company, corroborating the above statement. The business, it stated, was not successful. Thera had been a loss on the working of every year since the incorporation of the company. Taking the value of the goodwill and copyright of the business as £4OO, the losses amounted to £2,234 or thereabouts. No dividend had ever been paid by the company. Counsel explained that ia order to put an end to that state of things the company entered into an agreement with Messrs. Mackie for the future working of the company at an annual rental of £lOO. The effect of the agreement was that the company had no creditors at the present time. There were no trade creditors because the newspaper was being printed and published by Messrs. Mackie, and in his affidavit Mr. Withington stated that all the company's debts existing at the time of the agreement had been paid and with the exception of a few current expenses not exceeding £5O, the com- pany had now no debts.

• The Judge : That is very important. Mr. Preston said the material point arising from that was that up to the preseat the petition had not been advertised. The Court had power where it saw that no creditors would be affected to dispense with the adver- tisement and in view of the statement in the affidavit he asked his Honour to dispense with advertising the hearing of the petition. The Judge said he was disposed to grant the applica- tion except in regard to the omission of the words "and reduced." He would want some reason giving before he dispensed with them. Mr. Preston : The only reason I put forward is that there are no creditors in the case and nobody to whom notice of the reduction of capital would be of any materiality. It is a question of a domestic arrangement between the shareholders entirely. There are no outside creditors. _

--Th-e'-Ju-dge: Still, there might be. Mr. Preston : I do not think under the circumstances of the case there can be, because since August last the paper has been handed over to other persons altogether and they are running it at their expense for the time being, so that there can be no trade creditors. The court very often dispenses with the words "and reduced." Sometimes it orders that they-shall be used for fourteen days and sometimes for a month. Under the circumstances of this case, seeing that there are no creditors and that it is most improbable that there should he any, I ask you to dispense with the words "and reduced "altogether. The Judge said he was disposed to order that the words should be retained for thirty days. He confirmed the reduction of capital and approved the special minute of the company, with that qualification, and also agreed to dispense with advz.rtising the hearing of the petition. Instructions were also given for the sanctioning of the reduction of capital to be advertised.

THE LATE REV. E. J. WILLGOCKS. Memorial Decided Upon. A meeting of the subscribers to the fund for providing a memorial to the late Rev. E. J. Willcocks, M.A., for many years headmaster cf the Boteler Grammar School, was held at the Town Hall on Thurday evening to consider suggestions as to the form the memorial shall take. Mr. C. S. Burgess presided over a fair attendance which included Mr. J. H. Smethurst (hon. secretary) and Mr. C. D. Parkinson (hon. treasurer). in the circular convening the meeting it was stated that the committee were unanimously of the opinion that the money raised should be invested in the names of trustees and grants made from time to time on the recommenda- tion of the headmaster to boys going to Universities from the school and in addition that a small tablet should be placed in the school. Letters apologising for non-attendance were received from Sir Gilbert Greenall, Bart., Mr. J. Charlton Parr, Rev. Canon Stevenson, Mr. Arthur Down, Mr. J. C. Bate (Chester), Mr. F. A. Yeomans, and [Jr. 0. H. Cooke. Most of the writers cordially approved of the committee's suggestion. Mr. C. D. PARKINSON stated that the total amount of subscriptions received was £212 155., and the bank interest 4. id. After payinr, suadry expenses there was a balance of £235 13s. Id 7 The CIIAIRMAN said the subscriptions might be less than they originally hoped for but when he told them that no subscription had been more than 10 guineas and that they had received them as low as one shilling, he did not think the amount was unsatisfactory. Various schemes had been carefully discussed by the committee, and the proposed grants to University students and the ' erection of a tablet unanimously commended them- selves as being the most suitable memorial. He moved: That a portion of the money raised for providing a memorial to the late Rev. E. J. Willcocks be applied in the erection of a small brass tablet in the Boteler Grammar School, Warrington, to his memory. Mr. P.. Dosiox seconded and the motion was agreed to. The CIIAIRMIN then moved: That the balance of the money be invested in the names of trustees to be selected by the Memorial Committee and that new trustees, as necessity arises, be from time to time elected by the then existing tristees. Mr. A. BROWNE in seconding said many schemes were mooted and discussed at great length but it was thought that the one decided upon would have met the wishes of their late headmaster more than anything else.

Alderman BENNETT : E 3 it proposed to limit the grants to those who go to any particular University ? The Gaut-I.m AN : No, except that I take it we should limit it to Universities in the United Kingdom. It is not our intention to single out any pirticular University and we would not like to exclude such Universities as Manchester, Liverpool and Leeds. The resolution was passed. The CELVICOI iN moved and Mr. Walton seconded : That the income and any accumulation thereof to arise from the investment of the balanco be from time to time applied by way of grants to be made on the recommenda- tion of the headmaster for the time being of the Boteler Grammar School, subject to the approval of the trustees for the time being and in such sum or sums as the trustees may deem advisable, to any boy or boys going from the school or being at any University. Mr. CARACTIfERS pointed out that the fund would be of great benefit especially in a town like Warrington for when some students obtained exhibitions at Universities it was an exceedingly critical time for them as the expenses during the first term or two wore very heavy. In reply to Mr. Ferguson, the Chairman said it was not intended to confine the grant to Warrington boys but he approved the suggestion that students should have to attend the school a certain time before they became qualified. Mr.l3nowNE thought the matter might safely be left to the discretion of the trustees. The resolution was carried.
It was further resolved: That the memorial com- mittee or the trustees for the time being be empowered to embody the above resolutions in a trust deed if they so think fit. -

A hearty vote of thanks was accorded to the Mayor for allowing the use of the Council Chamber. Alderman BENNETT moved a vote of thanks to the Chairman, Mr. Smethurst, Mr. Parkinson and the Com- mittee for the interest they had taken in that labour of love, and the successful issue to which they had brought it He was sure their recommendations would commend themselves to all, and that in years to come boys who had the ability but perhaps not the means to enable them to succeed in life would be grateful to the sub- scribers and to the Committee. Mr. WILDING seconded, and the resolution was cordi- ally pissed.

div.head: ART EXHIBITION.
div.p: ART EXHIBITION.
WORKS OF THE LATE GEORGE SHEFFIELD.
Opening by Mr. A. H Crosfield, M.P.

The Museum Committee are to be congratulated ; upon having arranged such an interesting exhibition ' of the work of the late George Sheffield as is now to be seen lathe Municipal Art Gallery. Warring on is naturally proud of this tolented artist, whose genius is at last being generally recognized and appreciated, for although he was neither a native of Warrington nor yet a student at our School of Art, he had very close associations with the town and it was here that he did a great deal of his work and formed many friendships.. George Sheffield was born at Wigton, Cumberland, in 1839. His relations on both sides were of that district, and his uncle and namesake was a portrait painter of some local reputation. His parents moved, when George was quite young, to Warrington, and afterwards to Manchester, ,where he was apprenticed as a pattera designer, but he had no liking for such a career, and when his apprenticeship expired he at once and finally devoted himself to the art of landscape painting. During his apprenticeship and afterwards he rambled and sketched assiduously in South Lancashite and North Cheshire, and the result is abundantly shown in his work. A favourite sketching ground was along the Bridgewater Canal. He also travelled much, spending some time in Wales and Scotland, visiting Holland and Madeira, and crossing the Atlantic more than once. He was an exhibitor at the Royal Academy, 1872-90, and was a member of the Manchester Academy, where very many of his works were exhibited. After his marriage he lived at various times in the Alderley district, in the Isle-of- Man, at Warrington, and at Manchester, where he died in 1892. The outstanding features of Sheffield's genius were his wonderful imagination and his great facility of execution. It is said that his water-colour sketchings and paintings numbered thousands and his black-and-whites tens of thousands. It was something more than a theory with Sheffield that the medium was a matter of little moment to the genuine artist and he , demonstrated his view by the marvellous facility with which he could turn from oil to water colours and from crayons to charcoal. Oae of the finest black- and-white drawings he ever executed was presented to his friend Mr. T. Birtles and waiis accomplished without a single pause in an hour and seven minutes. Oa other occasions be dashed oil smaller and less important work in half the time. He once executed a ; large black-and-white drawing as an Infirmary con- tribution. It was begun and finished in the dining room of the late Mr. Thomas Morris, as a sort of object lesson, in the presence of a score of guests who were invited to witness tho per- formance. The friends about him were chatting and smoking and he did the same at intervals, finishing the drawing in about two hours and a lialf.lt was sold for something over £lO. The following lines, which were written for the " Examiner " when the artist ; was living in Warrington in 1885 will probably be read with renewed interest at the present moment : I George Sheaeld's a wonderful man— i A wonderful artist is he ; With his seeing eye and his cunning hand, He will make you a picture of sea or land— Of ship, or tower, or tree. He's at home on the roarinz main, When the load winds lash the deep ; He will paint you this, and then, again, He will show you the sea, one great smooth plain As calm as a child asleep. It is now a country scone— A river glowing and bright, With clumps of trees and a church between ; It is now a tale of what has been— A castle stormed in the night. In colour, or "black and white," He had ever a marvellous touch ; I've seen him lay "soot "on as black as night, And instantli turn it to clear moonlight— He once made a picture of " slutch." He's a comet amongst his kind— A spurner of bolts and bars, And whenever he leaves this earth behind, You will find he has mounted the wings of the wind. To go painting amid the stars. SOME OF THE PICTURES.

I The present exhibition —the first of Sheffield's work I ever held —consists of something like a hundred and I seventy works in oils, watercolour, sepia, charcoal and i pastel. It was opened on Tuesday afternoon by Mr. A. H. Crosfield, M.P.,and remains on view till June oth. I The pictures have been hung under the superintendence of Mr. T. Dirties, Mr. C. Madeley, the Town Clerk and other admirers of the artist's work, and convey a good impression of Sheffield's skill in many branches of art. On entering the room devoted to works in black and white,one's attention is immediately arrested by thirteen I early studies in pen and pencil, lent by Mr. G. W. Bullock, of Bowdon. They give striking evidence of that remarkable attention to detail which character- ised the whole of Sheffield's work. Mr. Edmondson lends a beautiful study in pencil outline of a park— trees and broken fenoes being admirably depicted. There are also six sketches in pencil intended for Christmas cards, and these have been lent by Mr. Abel Heywood, of Manchester. One of the most striking pictures is " The ancient mariner " lent by Mr. A. H. Croslield, M.P. It shows a vessel imprisoned among icebergs and conveys a wonderful suggestion of wierd desolation, aptly illustrating the lines in Coleridge's famous poem : And through the drifts, the snowy clifts, Did send a dismal sheen; No shapes of men nor beasts we ken, The ice was all between. Visitors should not fail to notice the beautiful " Shore scene," depicting the tide running out. This is the picture above mentioned which was executed in an hour and seven minutes for Mr. T. Birtles, by whom it is lent for this exhibition. A small upright "River Scene," belonging to Mr. Crosfield, is notable for feeling for tone and softness of atmospheric effect. A large drawinie of a fishing smack in a rough sea, lent by Alderman Bolton, is a very fine production, the wonderful sky effects at once exciting admiration. Another view from Alderman Bolton's collection shows Penketh Old Mill which used to stand between Penketh and Cuerdley, and it is considered a splendid specimen. Gecrge Sheffield was especially famed for his sepia drawings and this section of the exhibition is highly interesting. A beautiful study of a calm sea, lent by Alderman Bolton, is drawn with infinite care and attention to detail and there are some exquisite effects of light and shade. Another fine drawing on some- what similar lines is lent by Mr. Crosfielil. There is a very pretty study of an evening scene, with Mobberley Church in the background and trees in the foreground, while another striking work shows a troop of cavalry passing along a dusty Cheshire lane on a hot summer day. " The Ferry" lent by Mr. A. Webster is a charming picture of a winding river, with a punt and two figures to the fore, and an old mill in the background. An exquisite sea shore scene lent by Mr. H. Woolley conveys a fine impression of expanse and solitude. There are several pleasing scenes in Antwerp and Rotterdam an I another notable work is a sketch of Loo Rock, Madeira, winch the artist did when he visited Madeira along with his cousin, Dr. Shipman, M.P. who contributes several pictures to the exhibition. Sheffield's fondness for coast scenes is once more illustrated by a handsome sketch lent by Mr. Abel Heywood, of a rocky coast at even-tide, the light .effects being wonderfully conceived. "Shipping and Tug Boat," belonging to Mr. Crosfield, depicts sunrise at sea and a large sailing vessel about 'to be tagged away. A valuable collection - of early sepia drawings, lent by Mr. Edrnundson, of St. Annes- on-Sea, contsin a great deal of delicate treatment and show earnest work and a wonderful mastery of detail. In the water-colour section some of the best examples of Sheffield's talent are to be seen in the large picture from the Manchester Art Gallery, "rho Trough of the Sea," where the tumbling of the waves is expressed with a good deal of imaginative power ; and in another water colour of similar size and quality,:with a dark sky and sea and a band of light en the horizon. A beautiful stipple drawing "Shore scene " has some charming sunrise and colour effects. "Fairy scene, from tales of the genii," lent by Mr. Bullock, gives farther evidence of the artist's rare imaginative power. It is, of cOurse, an idealised picture with a beautiful river fringed with trees and bearing gondolas, while in the background are the graceful outlines of a temple. In the foreground appear numerous mysterious figures, in keeping with the general character of the work. Another picture which is bound to attract much attention is a view of a pier head by moonlight. An exquisite vignette "The picnic" lent by Mr. S. Shakeshaft is reminiscent of Turner, and another of "Lledr Valley " belonging to Mr. Crostield, is one of the gems of the collection. A view of the churchyard at Bettws-y-coed presents a charming rural scene.

Of the works in pastel, one of the most striking is "The night attack "lent by Mr. Crosfield. It depicts an attack on Norham Castle, and the grim fortress and the scene of confusion as the invaders storm it are finely realized. A view of Antwerp Harbour, lent by Alderman Bolton, is a brilliant piece of work, and a picture of some local interest, from Ur. Birtles' collection. shows a timber waggon passing along a road at Hartford on a snowy day. Three beautiful calm sea and beach studies, lent by Dr. Shipman, are la great acquisition to the exhibition ; and a " Winter Scene" lent by Mrs. Gan:lett has been generally admired.

There are seven oil paintings, one of the most attractive being " One hundred years ego," from the Manchester Art Gallery, representing a naval battle. One of the huge sailing vessels is on fire, and the troops are escaping in boots. Alderman Bolton sends a delightful view of Dover cliffs, with vessels beached on the sands below, and near it are hung two of Sheffield's earliest attempts -it oil painting, the object being to show how it is possible from very small beginnings to achieve a position of eminence in the world of art.

THE OPENING CERENIONY. INTERESTING SPEECH BY MR. A. H. CROSFIELD, M.P. SHEFFIELD'S WONDERFUL IMAGINATION. There was a large attendance at the opening of the exhibition on Tuesday afternoon by air. A. Ed. Crosfield M.P. Alderman Bennett (chairman of tke Museum Committee) presided. Aide-man Bf;NNHTT said that was, he believed, the first occasion on which Warrington had paid due and definite honour to its little company of famous artists, and it was a company of which any town might well be proud. (Applause.) First of all there was Hamlet Winstanley, in the middle of the eighteenth century, with his clever portraits of the Derby family and various classical paintings. Then, a century later, there was Thomas Robson, so meny of whose pictures now adorned their walls. Passing over, for-the moment, the name of the man in whose honour they were new assembled, they came to the famous group of students trained by the late Mr. J. Christmas Thompson—Warrington Wood, the sculptor ' • Henry Woods, 8.A., the brilliant painter of Venetian life and character, both born in Warrington ; and, last of the distinguished trio,Sir Luke H. Fildes,R.A..who received his early training here, and married Mr. Woods's sister, and of whose achievements in the realm of art it would be quite superfluous to speak. Nor must he on any account omit to mention the name of the late Mr. E. F. Brewtnall, another of Mr. Thompson's pupils, who painted the great picture on the other side of the room, or peer James Charles,both Warringtonians and each, alas ! cut down in the fullness of his man- hood, and just as he was beginning to reap the fame so well deserved.Bnt the torch had still been handed on,and he believed that the artistic reputation of the town was safe in the hands of the younger generation of local artists whom he need not now particularize, but in whom he had the utmost possible faith. He might, however, say in passing that last week he paid a flying visit to the Academy, and that upon its walls there were not lass than twelve exhibits by six artists who were more or less closely associated with his native town, (Applause). But that day they specially desired to celebrate the genius of George Sheffield. That was, he understood, the first representative exhibition of his works that had been held, and they trusted it would help to give him his place in the great Pantheon of British artists. (Applause). Much of his best work was done in Warrington. Many of those present were privileged to know him, and not a few could tell amazing tales of his facility in his high craft. And all of them could appreciate his genius and his versatility so well exemplified by the 171 specimens of his work in black and white, in sepia, in pastel, in water-colours and in oils, which all of them might see that afternoon. As he gazed upon the triumphs of his skill he was reminded of the words of Robert Browning in his lines on Andrea del Sarto " the faultless painter " : I can do with my pencil what I know, What I see, what at bottom of my heart I wish for, if I ever wish so deep— Do easily, too—when I say perfectly, I do not boast, perhaps. (Applause.) On behalf of his committee, he desired to very warmly thank the ladies and gentlemen who had so much assisted in getting them together that large and representative collection of George Sheflield's work. They were specially favoured in having with them on that interesting local occasion their worthy member, Mr. A. 11. Crostleld—(hear, hear)—who was himself a son of the old town, and was always anxious to advance its interests and promote its reputation. He had a double claim upon their gratitude that day, for not only had he consented to open their memorial exhibition, but he was one of the largest contributors to it. Mr. Cros- field was an authority on politics,golf,music—dare he say on Greek beauty ?—(laughter) —and last,and by no means least, on art ; and he was sure that they would join with him in giving him a most cordial welcome, and that they would listen to his remarks upon an artist whom he knew and much admired with the utmost interest and attention. He had the greatest possible pleasure in asking him to be good enough to open the ' exhibition. (Applause.) CnO3S'IELD, M.P. expressed his indebtedness to Alderman Bennett for the very kind—and he thought he might add, somewhat humorous—manner in which he had asked him to open the exhibition. lie thought Ithat Alderman Bennett and those in authority might have made a better choice, because he saw old friends 'of his in that room who were much more intimately laccputinted with both Sheffield himself and his work then he (Mr. Crosfield) could pretend to be. " I was a little surprised " continued Mr. Crosfield, " having met' I you, Alderman Bennett, the other day in an arena that , is,not quite so tranquil as we have here this afternoon --(laughter)—when you invited me to leave that some- what dusty turmoil of the political world in London to come down to this tranquil atmosphere—l might say the lofty empyrean of art. I have only one claim at all to fill this position, which it is a very great honour indeed to occupy, and that is the admiration I have always felt, since I was a little lad, for Sheffield's work—an admiration which I can assure all ray friends here only grows greater as the years roll on and as one gets to love, I can truly say like companions, the really fine specimens of Sheffield's work which I am lucky enough to possess. What strikes me in these works of Sheffield is the wonderful breadth of vision and the imagination which he exemplified in them—that on the one hand, and on the other such a subtle insight and such a tender feeling for all the shades and tones that you get in landscape painting. It is the range of knowledge and the variety of work which have always seemed to me quite remarkable in George Sheffield, and though I have only had a short time to look round this exhibition, I see that those features are illustrated very happily in the collection we have got together here. (Hear, hear.) I wish it had been a still more repre- sentative collection, but I really think we are very fortunate in what we have got." (Hear, hear.) Continuing Mr. Crosfield said he knew it was sug- gested that the exhibition of Sheffield's Works should take place in London. He hoped they would have an exhibition some thy in London but he thought it was a very happy idea that Warrington should come first—(applause)—because it was the town with which Sheffield and his family were so very long associated. The theory that everything in the kingdom should go to London was a very groat mistake. (Hear, hear). Concentration in London had gone pretty fir already and the place was getting a little unwieldy. It was therefore a very good thing that they should decentralise now and then and whatever might take place in London later on—and he for one had not the. faintest doubt that the day must come before long when Sheffield's marvellous genius would be appreciated— (applause)—he was so glad that they had had that , beautiful collection of pictures first of all in Warring- ton. (Applause). By way of comparing the contrasts in Sheffield's work, Mr. CrosfleH then directed attentioa to some of the pictures in the exhibition. If they took for instance," The Storming of Norhara Castle "they a ould see that although it wes done very much in the rough they at once had the spirit of the old scene—the fiehting spirit and the romance of the Middle Ages—conveyed to them with a dashing dire-devilry which showed the imagination of the artist. He could not recall any other picture of the kind that gave them the spirit of the scene better than that. He had had an opportunity, along with an old friend of his who had lent many pictures for which they were much obliged, of seeing in the other room that beautiful conception of Sheffield's taken from Coleridge's "Ancient Meriner,"and one could not imagine a greater contrast from the picture of Norham to that still scene, the subject of which w is "The frozen regions of the north." Of course,Sheifield's moonlight studies were always famous and merely as a tour de force in water colour work, some of those pictures were quite retharkable. MaCrosfleld instanced one, not included in the present exhibition, which was absolutely stipple and produced such marvellous midnight effects that when it was shown to Raskin he did not believe that anybody, excepting Turner, could have done such extraordinary water colour work. (Applause.) Sheffield was also famous for the chalk pictures on brown paper with which they were more familiar in Warrington. He (Mr. Crosaeld) was bound to say what appealed to him more than his water-colour work—speaking of moonlight pictures—were Sheffield's sepia drawings of midnight. He thought, not speaking as an expert but merely as a student of Sheffield's work, and one who admired it very greatly—some of the sepia work, both his studies at nighh and early morning, of sunset, landscape and seascape, was what Ruskin might have called insuper- able. A friend of his, who should be nameless, had a collection of sepias in one room, and gentlemen in Manchester who had the choice of One for a collection in that city could not make up their minds, after look- ing at them for half a day. which should be the treasure they would have. Alluding to a picture of the fairy glen in North Wales, Mr. Crosfield remarked that it was idealised and Sheffield, of course, like other great artists took little liberties at times in the arrangement and composition of his work. He spent six weeks on a picture of the fairy glen,and the fact was worthy of mention as illustrating the variety and con- trast of his work. His friend Mr. Birtles had told him a great deal about Sheffield's work, and he (Mr. Gros- field) was indebted to Mr. Birtles for some of the treasures he had got. Sheffield worked with amazing

rapidity, and he (Mr. Crosfield) knew he did one very striking and powerful work in black and white in one hour and seven minutes. As contrasted with that, he spent six weeks upon the fairy glen picture, washing out the sky thirteen times before he got the exact delicate shade he wanted. In that picture they had a water colour which in his humble op:nion was quite as wonderful, delicate and beautiful in its way as anything even of Turner's that he had ever seen. If they com- pared Sheffield's Conway Castle by sunset with Turner's Conway Castle by moonlight, he thought anybody would, in point of actual merit, hesitate betweea the two. (Applause.) Sheffield had done other work in Wales, and it was significant that the beautiful Welsh ' scenery attracted him as it attracted Taruer and David Cox. In conclusion, he would like to say a word or two about Sheffield's sea pieces. All who had seen his L marvellous sepias, whether they wore river or sea shore scenes, or whether the artist took them out on the briny and gave them a real good tossing, would feel that there Sheffield was really at home. They knew Sheffield was of a roving disposition and would often take ship and knock about the world a great deal, and he (ir. Crosfteld) supposed it was on the sea he got that I wonderfully intimate knowledge of sea craft and every- i thing that had to do with sea pieces. They would see ' 1 traces of it in his note book where he had gone in for the most minute studios of rigging and details of , shipping. In his sea pieces they had some of his very I finest conceptions. When they heard of the rapidity with which he did his work it was well to bear in mind the infinite amount of pains he took in graduating in his early days, the laborious work he had done which they would find in hundreds and even thousands of careful studies in his notebooks, all giving a wonderful command of detail,which enabled him to go to work with such rapidity later on. What was so striking in Sheffield was that while he had that splendid command of detail, and while he knew the value of detail, he never lost his sense of proportion and of relative values. They never found Sheffield letting the tree shut out the wood. With all that infinitely beautiful detail he gave , them in some of his work, he kept that sense of pro- portion which was just as valuable in art as it was fora trading community like Warrington. Ile (Mr. Crosfleld) sincerely hoped that beautiful collection of pictures might help to stimulate amongst them some of that breadth of vision and force of imagination which were two of Sheffield's greatest qualities. He thanked the gentlemen who had helpel to get together that collec- tion, which although not complete was very valuable and very delightful to them all. (Applaase). Mr. W. PETER RYLANDS,tiII proposing a vote of thanks to Mr. Crosfield, said he did not intend, after the inter- esting and critical survey which had been given of the works exhibited in that room, to add anything in that direction. Such an exhibition did honour to the artist as well as to the town, and it was no doubt on that account that Mr. Crosfield, who took so much interest in everything that related to his native town, had come to Warrington to open the exhibition. (Jeer, hear and applause). Ile thought they owed Mr. Cros- field something more than a vote of thanks, which they naturally accorded to him for coming to Warrington to open the exhibition, for the address he had given them showed, as they might have expeeted from their know- ledge of him,an intimate love of art and an acquaintance with the subject which had been by no means treated in a perfunctory manner. (Hear, hear and applause). Mr. C. E. PARKER, in seconding, said:his association with the district was not sufficiently lengthy to enable him to know anything of Sheffield's work personally,but he had been connected for a number of years with a village in which Sheffield first showed that artistic power in the Penketh School which developed so much in later years. It was in that village that he did a great deal of work. His (Mr. Parker's) wife had just been pointing out to him a picture representing a wintry afternoon, and she had expressed her lively recollection of the time when, as a girl, she looked over Mr. Sheffield's shoulder and saw the scene depicted grow under his hand. (Applause.) The picture in question was done in about an hour. Mr. Croseeld had shown them by his critical and appreciative remarks about Sheffield that they could not have had a reore appropriate gentleman to open the exhibition. (Hear, heir, and applause.) Alderman BENNETT said the exhibition would be con- tinued until the 6th June, and they wished to make it as widely known as possible. They hoped to have some of Sheffield's works in their pormaneat collection, and, if the exhibition was a success, as time weat on to do a similar honour to other eminent Warringtonians who han achieved distinction in the world of art.(Applause.) The resolution was then put and carried with heartiness.

Mr. Crosfield, in reply, said nobody was more sensible than he was of his incapacity to do justice to so great a subject, because the more one looked into Sheffield's works the more one was struck with his range and wonderfnl variety and capacity. That exhibition would help to bring his memory more to the frant and give him, though a little late in tho day—hut it was better late than never—that place in the world of art which his genius surely and certainly deserved. (Applause).

div.head: TO HELP THE VETERANS. Lady Mayoress of ii-varpool's Appeal at Warrington.
div.p: TO HELP THE VETERANS. Lady Mayoress of ii-varpool's Appeal at Warrington.

A representative meeting of ladies of Warrington and district convened by the Mayoress (Mrs. Smethurst) was held at the Town llall, on Thursday afternoon, for the purpose of considering what assistance could be rendered by them in connection with the appeal on behalf of the Crimean and Indian Mutiny Veterans. There were also present : his Worship the Mayor (Mr. Alderman Sraethurst)who presided,the Lady NI tyoress of Liverpool(Mrs.Caton),and the Rev.Csnon Willis. Letters of apology were raid from a number of prominent ladies who were unable to attend, but who promised their assistance and support. At the outset the MAYOR, in thanking those present for their attendance stated that there were 17 Veterans in Warrington and that over 1,000 ciroulars had been issued to residents appealing for subscriptions but that up to the present £1.4 represented the only response. lie felt sure however that as a result of that meeting a substantial sum would be raised.

The LIDY MAYORESS OP LIVERPOOL (wllO was intro- duced by His Worship) then explained at considerable length the steps taken in Liverpool towards furthering the appeal and recited instances of hardship borne by Veterans which had been brought to her notice amongst which her Ladyship referred to the case of one old Veteran who regularly pawned his medals in order to buy bread and on receipt of his pension every quarter redeemed them. As an instance of self-denial, her Ladyship mentioned the case of another very infirm man who had whilst in good positions spout all his savings in supporting a widowed sister and bringing up her family of 7 children, leaving himself in his old days in very straightened circumstances. Such cases as these, her Ladyship remarked, ought to make us feel for the old soldier, is it not, she asked, only just that if England expects every man to do his duty, she should in turn fulfil her duty to him? (Applause.) Some people would say that the Government should provide for the Veterans but that was only putting off the question and in the meantime the men would die. In order to raise funds which were urgently needed, Lord Ro'aerts had arranged to have a groat National fAte at Chelsea. Scenes of Crimean and Indian Mutiny ,would be reproduced, and in the Hospital grounds a bazaar would be held. West Lancashire would be represented by a stall at the bazaar, and the moneys realised by the sale of goods sent from Warrington and District would be devoted to the relief of their veterans. In conclusion her Ladyship strongly appealed for support either monetary, or for articles for the forthcoming Bazaar. The Rev. CANON Minis expressed the pleasure it would afford him in doing all in his power for such a deserving cau-le, and said how much they all appreciated the interest shown by the Lady Mayoress in this most impartant work.

After discussion it was arranged that appeals should he made for articles for the West Lancashire stall at the National Fête to be sent to the Town Hall not later than Monday the 22rid of JIIIIO. A request was made that all goods sent in should be priced by the donors. -

Miss SYLVIA BRO\DBENT WAS appointed Hon. Secre- ta.y of the Ladies' Committee. On the proposition of Nirs. BR9 ton ENT, seconded by Mrs. ArtairraGß, a hearty vote of thanks was accorded to the Lady Mayoress of Liverpool for her attendance.

Warrington Philomathic Society. The annual meeting of the above society was held i on Wednesday in Gregory's Cafe, Butterrnarket-street. The President took the chair at 7.30 p.m. The secretary in his report said that the members had taken a great interest in the work of the Society as was shown by the attendances, the average bein,r; 61 per cent. The lectures had been most interesting and the debates very keen. The thanks of the society were due to Mr. W. IT. Stansii.tld for a lecture and to Mr. G. 11. Crosileld for opening a debate. He hoped the membership would continue to increase, as he thought the society would in time fill a long felt want ia Warrington.—A vote of thanks was. proposed to the retiring officers and council for their services during the past session.—The President,. in the course of his reply, said that he did not accept his office to receive a panegyric at the close of the session, but because he always wished to do all in his power to further those principles for which the Philomathic Society so conspicuously stood. It could not be denied that the Society had made a most distinct step in advance during the session, to halt now would mean death. The Society had made itself felt and largely increased its influence in the town. Con sequently the new officers would commence their work with a grave sense of responsibility. He thanked the members for their appreciation, and wished the new Council every success. The officers for next session— which opens in October,—were elected as follows : President: Mr. J. Herbert Mason ; Vice-President : Councillor James Ball ; Treasurer: Mr. IL H. Mellor ; Secretary : Mr. Sydney C. Burgess 14 Winmarleigh- street.

div.head: ROYAL COURT THEATRE. ---- " His House in Order."
div.p: ROYAL COURT THEATRE. ---- " His House in Order."

Warrington theatre-goers have been aff .rded an exceptional treat this week by the management of the Royal Court Theatre, who have provided for their delectation one of the greatest of Pinero's problem plays, "His House in Order." It was only last autumn that Mr. George Alexander and Miss Irene Vanbrug,h were touring the country with this famous play after a run of 421 consecutive performances in London. Toe present company is a worthy successor to the original one and is being toured by Mr. H. Ralph Kimpton. for many years stage manager to Mr. Alexander himself. "His House in Order "is one of those plays that would be a ghastly failure in the hands of any but experienced and intelligent actors. Piuero's comedy is a, subtle, and his darker shades so delicate, that they necessitate artistic expression to be appreciated at all. We have seen nothing since the 'first appearance of "The Gay Lord Quex " to come up to "His Mince in Order," and even now we should be inclined to give the palm to the earlier pro- duction. But the play of the moment is certainly worthy of the flattering things said about it. " His House in Order " has a capacity for sustaining the closest interest, and arousing the liveliest specula- tion among the uninitiated as to its ending. The story has a heroine, but no love romance, which is in itself an unusual feature. Nina, second wife of Filuaer Jesson, M.P., is the lady round whom the play is woven. She is altogether an attrac- tive young person, last unfortunately her husband and ' hi 3 relatives persist in viewing her through the glamour of the perfect first wife, Annabel Mary. Nina has, consequently, a hideou3 time, with petty restrictions and snubs at every turn. The deceased wife's sister is even installed as general manager of Jes3on's menage with full powers to keep " his house ,in order." Upon these warring elemente comes Hilary Jesson, brother of Filmer, a diplomat from , abroad. He at once appreciates the distracting Iposition of affairs, and endeavours with sympathetic i intervention to secure for Mistress Nina her rightful Iplace in the household. But the spirit of the departed lAnnabel Mary seems ever to cast a chill over his ' efforts. The crowning humiliation results in Nina'a fierce rebellion, and she appears only to have made matters worse when Fate plays the tramp card into her hand. The letters of the dead wife come into her possession and Nina makes the thrilling, and not unpleasing discovery that Annabel Mary had not been the lily-white hen her husband and her family had always thought her. She had a secret —which would have gone to the grave with her but for the letters. At first Nina. is for using the weapon thus placed in her hand, and who would deny her right to do so seeing the mortification of spirit to which she had been subjected ? She has the power to make Geraldine and the other Ridgeleys crawl, but in the moment of inward triumph Hilary comes upon her. He is stunned for the moment by the discovery, but using superior to the sataller impulses of life he reasons with Nina in a speech of remarkable power and persuasiveness. She sees with his eyes and decides upon the chivalrous act of renunciation which compels nearly every woman in the audience to say " I wouldn't." She will not dis- close the paternity of the " sainted " first wife's son, great as the temptation is to smash the pare white image cherished so gloatingly by her husband and the Ridgeleys. It looks as if she is to suffer to the end, but Fate again intervenes and Hilary tells Filmer. Then tha scales fall from the husband's eyes.He leaves the dead to the dead and honours the living in a manly declaration. The deceased uife's family are I spared the truth, and the one regret of the play is that .- they are not made to drain the bitter cup to the dresasa. Mr. Pinero made the Ridgeleys very odious, and one , regrets to see them let off so lightly. in the trying) role of Nina, Miss Nora Harker greatly distinguishesi herself. She is vivacious, dramatic, and spirited as :j occasion demands and altogether pleased a discriminat- ing audience. Mr. Herbert Beaumant proves himself a worthy successor to Mr. Alexander in the part of ' Hilary Jesson, and in his great opportunities in acts 3 and 4 he displays histrionic abilities of an enviable order. A capital pourtrayal of FilaterJessoa is given by Mr. James C. Taylor. The Ridgeleys are all good, and especially Geraldine (Kiss Barbara Mendyll) and Sir Daniel (Mr. Langford Brown). The company is so strong that it is difficult to particularise further, but a good word should be said for Miss Doris Lorraine who acts the French maid to perfection and "contrives to look smart even after three years in England." The bluff and hearty Mayor is capitally represented by Mr. Frederick Sandy, and Mr. Harold Gee makes the most of the unpalatable role of Major Maurewarde. Kiss Lila Wandle is amusing as the precocious Derek Jesson, and "his" obvious attachment to Maurewarde throws an interesting side-light on the play. NEXT WEEK'S PROGRAMME. ! Next week Mr. Frank Undo and Miss Marion Wakeford, supported by a powerful company, will present the great domestic drama " Home, sweet home." The story is one of the deepest interest and fully realises the truth of the world-famous song. The success achieved on its first production at the Shake- speare Theatre, London, has been repeated throughout the provinces. In a letter to the author (Mr. F. Lindo) Mr. Hall Caine says : " I wish you every possible success with your new play and I think you have chosen the happiest of titles for it. . . . There is a sweet proverb which says ` Home is a full cup' and if your new ploy helps to stipaulate the home-sense among the English people, in whom it has always been strong, it need not fear the criticism that it may thereby foster any form of little Englandism." The company his bean selected with great care and includes the charming actress Miss Marion Wakeford in her original creation" Joan."

Dispute About a Business. At the Warrington County Court on Thursday, before his Honour Judge Shiress Will, KM., Joseph Cartwright, 21, Percy-street, sued E. Murphy, 31, Garabaldi-street, for £l, being_the amount of a deposit paid to the defendant and £4 as. damages for alleged breach of contract.-llr. A. Browne appeared for the plaintiff and Mr. T. E. Knowles far the defendant.— Plaintiff's case was that in response to a newspaper advertisement of a "nice little mixed business for die- posal,"his wife saw the defendan•;'s wife who agreed to sell a business in Butternaarket-street for £lO. It was arranged that plaintiff should take possession on March 2nd, and a deposit of £1 was paid. On March 2nd plaintiff received a letter from defendant in • which he stated : "Considering the bather and expense I have been put t) in this matter, I am justified in keeping the deposit. The business is still open for you, should you agree to buy it." Another interview took place and at defendant's suggestion it was agreed that plaintiff should not take possession until March 16th. On March 10th, plaintiff discovered to his surprise that another party —a Mrs. Crawford—had entered into possession and it transpired that she had paid £l5 for the business. Plaintiff had given notice to quit his house and had packed his furniture ready to remove.—Plaintiff's wife , his son Albert, and his daughter Ann Sarah Chapman r. were called to support this statement and Mrs. Crawford testified to having paid £l5 for the, business. - The defence was that it was plaintiff's own' fault that ha did not obtain the business as the- plaintiff, his son and his daughter had all told defend-.r ant that the premises were not suitable and therefore the contract was at an end. Plaintiff asked for the return of the deposit and that caused the defendant to write the letter, as beheld that plaintiff had forfeited . 44 the money.—There was a direct conflict of evidence on ' the facts, but his Honour in giving judgment said be attached great importance to the testimony of Mr. Walter Twiss, on behalf of the landlord of the shop. A who stated that plaintiff told him he did not intend to ~ take possession as there was not sufficient room at the ; back of the premises to erect a shed. -Judgment was 1 given for the defendant with costs.

THE SCOTTISH NATIONAL, EXHIBITION. The above exhibition opened by Prince Arthur Of Connaught is acknowledged a triumphant success. It stands on the Saugheon Hall Estate, Edinburgh, and no exhibition north of the Tweed has ever roused such enthusiasm. Its aims and scope are of a far wider and more comprehensive nature than merely Scottish for there is exemplified all that is best in art, science, literature, and industry from his Majesty .'s dominions all the world over. The exhibition will remain open until October.A great day will be June 13th when Scotland's great national pageant is to be cele- brated All sorts of athletic and musical contests have been arranged. We hope to he able to give some descriptive notes on the Exhibition next week.

TRADES AND LABOUR COUNCIL. The Housing Question. The monthly meeting of the Warrington Trades and Labour Council was held in the I.L.P. rooms on Tuesday evening, the President (Mr. W.ll. Richardson), in the chair. Owing to the absence of the Secretary Orr. E. Plinston}, Mr. MoORFIELD read a letter from Mr. W. H. J. Jenkins, which stated that in the past various secretaries of their branches bad taken collecting cards in aid of the funds of the Poor Children's Camp and asking for a list of those secretaries. The SECRETARY was instructed to furnish the list. Mr. MALONE moved that.the Workingmen's National Housing Council be asked to furnish their objects end advantages to tbe Trades Council with a view that War- rington might have a Committee in support of the Housing Question. Mr. How LISTON moved that the Executive Comm itt ce take the matter up and get all the information possible, and bring it before the Council. Mr. COTTERILL seconded that amendment iwhich was carried. Mr. MOORWIELD moved "That in view of the fact that the Royal Londxs Friendly society Board of Managemept are making strenuous attempts at the present time to convert the society into a mutunl assurance company against the wishes of vast numbtrs of its members and the interests of its agents, this Council strongly condemns such action and pledgrs itself to oppose and by every legitimate means in its power to defeat such an object and to forward cozies of this resolution to the Royal London Society, the National Labour Party, local members, and. the Registrar General." Mr. LEECII secoctded- and the resoldtion was carried unanimously.
